It has been said that the couches here are a metaphor for the women of Paradise, and their being raised means that they are upon thrones (al-ara'ik), or that they are elevated in rank in beauty and perfection.

﴿Indeed We produced them with a production﴾, meaning We created them with a new creation without procreation. It has also been said that what is meant is the women of the children of Adam, and the meaning is that God, glorified is He, returned them after death to the state of youth. Although the women have not been mentioned before, they have entered among the companions of the right hand. As for the view of the one who said that the raised couches are the women themselves, the reference of the pronoun is clear.

﴿And We made them virgins﴾, ﴿untouched by man or jinn before them﴾.

﴿Loving, of equal age﴾. Ruba is the plural of 'arub, who is the one who is affectionate toward her husband.

Al-Mubarrad said: she is the one who loves her husband, and from this is the saying of Labid:
And in the tent is one who is loving, not indecent, whose buttocks are full, whose light dazzles the sight.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: she is the one good in speech.

Al-Jumhur read it with a damma on the 'ayn and the ra'. Hamzah and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with sukun on the ra', and both are dialects for the plural of fa'ul. Al-atrab are those who are of the same birth and the same age.

Mujahid said: atraban means similar and of the same forms.

Al-Suddi said: atraban in character, with no hatred or envy among them.

His saying: ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾ is connected to "We produced them," or to "We made them," or to "atraban." The meaning is that God produced them for their sake, or created them for their sake, or they are equal to the companions of the right hand in age. Or it is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are for the companions of the right hand.

﴿A company from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿a company from the later ones﴾. This refers back to His saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand: what of the companions of the right hand?﴾, meaning they are a company from the earlier ones and a company from the later ones. The tafsir of thulla has already been given when mentioning the foremost. The meaning is that they are a group, or a community, or a party, or a portion, from the earlier ones, who are from Adam until our Prophet (ﷺ), and a group, or a community, or a party, or a portion, from the later ones, who are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and al-Dahhak said: ﴿A company from the earlier ones﴾ means from the foremost of this community, and ﴿a company from the later ones﴾ means from this community, from its last part.

Then, when He, glorified is He, finished with what He had prepared for the companions of the right hand, He began to mention the companions of the left (ashab al-shimal) and what He had prepared for them, saying: ﴿And the companions of the left hand: what of the companions of the left hand?﴾ The discussion of the grammatical construction of this and of the magnification within it is as was mentioned for the companions of the right hand.

His saying: ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾ is either a second predicate of the companions of the left hand, or the predicate of an omitted subject. Al-samum is the heat of the Fire, and al-hamim is water extremely hot, and its meaning has already been explained.

It has been said that al-samum is the hot wind that enters the pores of the body.

﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾. Al-yahmum is the form yafa'ul from al-ahamm, which is black. The Arabs say "aswad yahmum" when something is intensely black. The meaning is that they resort to shade, but they find it a shade of black smoke from the smoke of Hell.

It has also been said that it is derived from al-hamm, which is fat blackened by the burning of fire.

It has also been said that it is derived from al-humum, which is charcoal.

Al-Dahhak said: the Fire is black and everything in it is black.

Then He described this shade by His saying: ﴿Neither cool nor pleasant﴾, meaning it is not like other shades that are cool, but rather it is hot because it comes from the smoke of the fire of Hell.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "nor pleasant" means it has no pleasant appearance, and everything that has no good in it is not pleasant. Al-Dahhak said: "nor pleasant" means nor sweet.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs make karim follow anything from which they negate a quality, intending blame by it. They say: "He is not fat nor karim," and "This house is not spacious nor karimah."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned their deeds for which they deserved punishment, saying: ﴿Indeed they were before that affluent (mutrafin)﴾. This clause gives the reason for what precedes it, meaning: indeed they were, before this punishment that descended upon them, affluent in this world, that is, enjoying what was not lawful for them. Al-mutraf is the one who lives in luxury.

Al-Suddi said: "mushrikin" (polytheists). It has also been said: "mutakabbirin" (arrogant). The first is more apt.

﴿And they used to persist in the great violation﴾. Al-hinth is sin, meaning they persisted in the great sin.

Al-Wahidi said: the people of tafsir said: by it is meant shirk, meaning they did not repent from shirk. This was also the view of al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: it is the great sin from which they did not repent.

Al-Sha'bi said: it is the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus).

﴿And they used to say: "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers, the earliest?"﴾ The hamza in the two places is for denial and disbelief. This matter has already been discussed in al-Saffat and in surah al-Ra'd. The meaning is that they denied and considered it unlikely that they would be raised after death when they had become bones and dust. What is meant is that their flesh and skins became dust and their bones became decayed and crumbling. The governing element of the adverbial phrase is what is indicated by "mab'uthun," because what follows an interrogative does not govern what precedes it. That is: shall we be raised when we die? and so on.

﴿Or our forefathers, the earliest?﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿mab'uthun﴾, because the separation between them is by the hamza. The meaning is that the resurrection of their earliest forefathers is more remote, because their death came earlier. It is also read "wa-aba'una" (with a different reading).

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to answer them and to reject their disbelief, saying: ﴿Say: "Indeed the earliest and the latest﴾ ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day﴾." That is: say to them, O Muhammad, that indeed the earliest of the nations and the latest of them, of whom you are part, will surely be gathered after the resurrection ﴿to the appointed time of a known day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers﴾. This and what follows are part of what falls under the saying, and it is conjoined to "indeed the earliest." He, glorified is He, described them with two ugly attributes: straying from the truth, and denying it.

﴿You will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum﴾, meaning: you will surely eat in the Hereafter from a tree whose appearance is hateful and whose taste is hateful. Its tafsir has already been given in surah al-Saffat. The first min is for the beginning of the limit, and the second is explanatory. It is also permissible that the first min is superfluous and the second is explanatory, or that the second is superfluous and the first is for the beginning.

﴿And filling your bellies with it﴾, meaning you will fill your bellies with the tree of zaqqum because of the severe hunger that will befall you.

﴿Then you will drink on top of it from the boiling water﴾. The pronoun in "on it" refers to the zaqqum, and hamim is water whose heat has reached its extreme. The meaning is: you will drink on top of the zaqqum, immediately after eating it, from scalding water. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to "tree," because it can be masculine or feminine. It is also possible that it refers to the eating that is indicated by His saying "you will surely eat." It has been read "min shajarah" (from a tree) in the singular.

﴿So you will drink as thirsty camels drink (shurb al-him)﴾. Al-Jumhur read "shurb al-him" with a fatha on the shin. Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah read it with a damma, and Mujahid and Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi read it with a kasra. These are dialects. Abu Zayd said: I heard the Arabs say it with a damma on the shin, a fatha, and a kasra. Al-Mubarrad said: the fatha is on the basis of the verbal noun (masdar), and the damma is the noun of the verbal noun (ism al-masdar). Al-him are thirsty camels that are not satisfied because of a disease that afflicts them. This clause explains what precedes it: meaning, your drinking will not be ordinary drinking, but like the drinking of al-him, which are thirsty and are not quenched by drinking water. The singular of al-him is ahyam, and the feminine is hayma'.

Qays ibn al-Mulawwah said:
It is said that the disease of love (hiyam) afflicted him, and my soul knew the place of my cure.

Al-Dahhak, Ibn 'Uyaynah, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan said: al-Hiym is the easy land with sand, and the meaning is that they drink as this land drinks water and no trace of it appears in it.

[p-1448] Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: al-Hiyam with a damma is the most intense thirst, and al-hiyam is like madness from love. Al-hiyam is a disease that takes camels so that they wander the land and do not graze. One says a she-camel is hayma'. Al-hayma' is also the desert with no water in it. Al-hiyam with a fatha is sand that does not hold together in the hand because of its softness, and its plural is huyum like qadhal and qudhul. Al-hiyam with a kasra is thirsty camels.

﴿This is their hospitality on the Day of Judgment﴾. Al-Jumhur read "nuzuluhum" with two dammas. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Muhaysin with one damma and a sukun. It has already been mentioned that al-nuzul is what is prepared for a guest and is the first thing he eats. The Day of Judgment is the Day of Recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that what has been mentioned of the tree of zaqqum and the drink of boiling water is what is prepared for them, and what they eat on the Day of Resurrection. In this there is mockery of them, because nuzul is what is prepared for guests as an honour for them. A similar example is His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 56, verses 27–56 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Hakim, who declared it sound (ṣaḥīḥ), and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "Allah benefits us through the Bedouins and their questions." "A Bedouin came one day and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, a harmful tree is mentioned in the Qur'an, and I did not think there was a tree in Paradise that harms its companion.' He said: 'And what is it?' He said: 'The lote tree (sidr), for it has thorns.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Did Allah not say: ﴿Among thornless lote trees﴾? Allah will remove its thorns and place in the stead of each thorn a fruit, and it will bring forth fruit which splits open to reveal seventy-two kinds of food, no two of which resemble each other.'"

Ibn Abi Dawud, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿUyaynah ibn ʿAbd al-Sulami, who said: "I was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) when a Bedouin came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I hear you mention a tree in Paradise, and I know of no tree with more thorns than it—meaning the acacia (ṭalḥ).' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah will place in the stead of each of its thorns a fruit like the testicle of a castrated ram, and in it there will be seventy kinds of food, no one of which resembles another.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿among thornless lote trees﴾ that he said: "He removed its thorns and made it heavy with fruit."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through several chains from him (Ibn ʿAbbas), who said: "The makhdud is that which has no thorn in it."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd also narrated from him: "The makhdud is the laden one that has no thorn in it."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib regarding His words ﴿and acacia laden with fruit﴾ that he said: "It is the banana (mawz)."

al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Hurayrah the same.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri the same.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib that he recited ﴿and banana (ṭalʿ) laden with fruit﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from Qays ibn ʿUbbad, who said: "I recited to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib '﴿and acacia laden with fruit﴾,' and ʿAli said: 'What is the matter with the acacia? Do you not recite ﴿and banana (ṭalʿ)﴾?' Then he said: ﴿banana arranged in tiers﴾ [Qaf 50:10]. It was said to him: 'O Commander of the Faithful, shall we erase it from the Mushaf?' He said: 'The Qur'an is not to be stirred up today.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿arranged in tiers﴾ that he said: "Some of it is upon others."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Indeed in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider can travel for a hundred years without crossing it. Recite if you wish: ﴿and extended shade﴾."

al-Bukhari and others narrated something similar from the hadith of Anas.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated something similar from the hadith of Abu Saʿid.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), al-Nasai, and others narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His words ﴿and raised couches﴾ that he said: "Their height is as the distance between the heaven and the earth, and the journey between them is five hundred years."

After narrating it, al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib (strange) hadith, which we do not know except from the narration of Rishdin ibn Saʿd." And Rishdin is weak (ḍaʿīf).

al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His words ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special production﴾: 'The produced ones are those who were in the world, old women, blear-eyed and with discharge.'"

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: "It is gharib, and Musa and Yazid are weak."

al-Tayalisi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Qani', and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth narrated from Salamah ibn Yazid al-Juʿfi, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say regarding His words ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special production﴾: 'They are the previously married and the virgins who were in the world.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "He created them other than their first creation."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿virgins﴾ that he said: "Maidens."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth narrated through the chain of ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿loving, of equal age﴾ that he said: "Loving: ʿawashiq (passionate toward their husbands)." And regarding "equal age" he said: "Equal in age, meaning equal."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿loving﴾ that he said: "Passionate toward their husbands, and their husbands are passionate toward them." Regarding "equal age" he said: "At one age, thirty-three years."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also that he said: "The ʿarub is the one who is coquettish toward her husband."

Musaddad in his Musnad (a collection arranged by companion), Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a fair chain (ḥasan) from Abu Bakrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His words ﴿a multitude from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a multitude from the later ones﴾ that he said: "Both of them are from this Ummah."

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Musaddad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakrah regarding His words ﴿a multitude from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a multitude from the later ones﴾ that he said: "They are both from this Ummah."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn ʿAdi, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said with a weak chain, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿a multitude from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a multitude from the later ones﴾ that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Both of them are from my Ummah.'"

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The two multitudes together are from this Ummah."

al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, narrated from Ibn (p-1449) ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾ that he said: "Of black smoke," and in another wording: "Of the smoke of Hell."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿drinking like thirsty camels﴾ that he said: "The thirsty camels."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 56, verses 27–56 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glorified is He, finished mentioning the states of the foremost (al-sabiqun) and what He had prepared for them of lasting bliss, He mentioned the states of the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand: what of the companions of the right hand?﴾ We have already explained the grammatical construction (i'rab) of this statement, and the magnification and exaltation contained in this interrogative clause. It is the predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada'), which is "companions of the right hand."

His saying: ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns﴾ is a second predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are among lote-trees without thorns. Al-sidr is a kind of tree, and al-makhdud is that whose thorns have been removed, meaning cut off, so that there are no thorns on it.

Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said, describing Paradise:
Indeed the gardens in the Gardens are shady, in them are the maidens, and their lote-trees are thornless.

Al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: indeed al-sidr al-makhdud is that which is laden with fruit (al-mawqur hamlan).

﴿And acacia arranged in tiers﴾. Most of the exegetes said that al-talh in the verse is the banana tree (shajar al-mawz).

A group said: it is not the banana tree, but the well-known talh, which is the greatest of the trees of the Arabs.

Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is a large tree that has thorns.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-talh is Umm Ghaylan, and it has a pleasant blossom. So they were addressed and promised what they love, except that its excellence over what is in this world is like the excellence of all that is in Paradise over what is in this world.

He said: it is possible that it is in Paradise but its thorns have been removed.

Al-Suddi said: the acacia of Paradise resembles the acacia of this world, but it has fruit sweeter than honey. Al-mandud is that which is piled up, whose beginning and end are arranged with fruit, and which has no protruding branches.

Masruq said: the trees of Paradise, from their roots to their branches, are arranged in tiers with fruit entirely; whenever a fruit is taken, another better than it grows in its place.

﴿And spreading shade﴾, meaning lasting and enduring, which does not cease and which the sun does not cancel.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: the Arabs call everything long that does not end "mamdud" (extended). From this is His saying: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shade?﴾ [al-Furqan: 45]. And the whole of Paradise is shade, with no sun in it.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it means the shade of the Throne. From the Arabs' use of "mamdud" for what is enduring and does not end is the saying of Labid:
Grief overcame patience, though I was not one to be overcome; a long-lasting, enduring time.

﴿And water poured out﴾, meaning flowing continuously by night and day wherever they wish, not ceasing for them. It is poured out, which God pours out in its channels. The origin of al-sakb is pouring; one says "sakaba-hu sakban", meaning he poured it.

﴿And fruit abundant﴾, meaning varied kinds, multiplied.

﴿Neither cut off﴾ at any time, as the fruits of this world are cut off at certain times, ﴿nor forbidden﴾, meaning they are not withheld from whoever wishes them at any time or in any condition. Rather, they are prepared for whoever wishes them, and nothing stands between him and them.

Ibn Qutaybah said: it means they are not prohibited to them as the gardens of this world are guarded against.

﴿And raised couches﴾, meaning raised, some of them above others, or raised upon couches.

It has been said that the couches here are a metaphor for the women of Paradise, and their being raised means that they are upon thrones (al-ara'ik), or that they are elevated in rank in beauty and perfection.

﴿Indeed We produced them with a production﴾, meaning We created them with a new creation without procreation. It has also been said that what is meant is the women of the children of Adam, and the meaning is that God, glorified is He, returned them after death to the state of youth. Although the women have not been mentioned before, they have entered among the companions of the right hand. As for the view of the one who said that the raised couches are the women themselves, the reference of the pronoun is clear.

﴿And We made them virgins﴾, ﴿untouched by man or jinn before them﴾.

﴿Loving, of equal age﴾. Ruba is the plural of 'arub, who is the one who is affectionate toward her husband.

Al-Mubarrad said: she is the one who loves her husband, and from this is the saying of Labid:
And in the tent is one who is loving, not indecent, whose buttocks are full, whose light dazzles the sight.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: she is the one good in speech.

Al-Jumhur read it with a damma on the 'ayn and the ra'. Hamzah and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with sukun on the ra', and both are dialects for the plural of fa'ul. Al-atrab are those who are of the same birth and the same age.

Mujahid said: atraban means similar and of the same forms.

Al-Suddi said: atraban in character, with no hatred or envy among them.

His saying: ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾ is connected to "We produced them," or to "We made them," or to "atraban." The meaning is that God produced them for their sake, or created them for their sake, or they are equal to the companions of the right hand in age. Or it is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are for the companions of the right hand.

﴿A company from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿a company from the later ones﴾. This refers back to His saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand: what of the companions of the right hand?﴾, meaning they are a company from the earlier ones and a company from the later ones. The tafsir of thulla has already been given when mentioning the foremost. The meaning is that they are a group, or a community, or a party, or a portion, from the earlier ones, who are from Adam until our Prophet (ﷺ), and a group, or a community, or a party, or a portion, from the later ones, who are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and al-Dahhak said: ﴿A company from the earlier ones﴾ means from the foremost of this community, and ﴿a company from the later ones﴾ means from this community, from its last part.

Then, when He, glorified is He, finished with what He had prepared for the companions of the right hand, He began to mention the companions of the left (ashab al-shimal) and what He had prepared for them, saying: ﴿And the companions of the left hand: what of the companions of the left hand?﴾ The discussion of the grammatical construction of this and of the magnification within it is as was mentioned for the companions of the right hand.

His saying: ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾ is either a second predicate of the companions of the left hand, or the predicate of an omitted subject. Al-samum is the heat of the Fire, and al-hamim is water extremely hot, and its meaning has already been explained.

It has been said that al-samum is the hot wind that enters the pores of the body.

﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾. Al-yahmum is the form yafa'ul from al-ahamm, which is black. The Arabs say "aswad yahmum" when something is intensely black. The meaning is that they resort to shade, but they find it a shade of black smoke from the smoke of Hell.

It has also been said that it is derived from al-hamm, which is fat blackened by the burning of fire.

It has also been said that it is derived from al-humum, which is charcoal.

Al-Dahhak said: the Fire is black and everything in it is black.

Then He described this shade by His saying: ﴿Neither cool nor pleasant﴾, meaning it is not like other shades that are cool, but rather it is hot because it comes from the smoke of the fire of Hell.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "nor pleasant" means it has no pleasant appearance, and everything that has no good in it is not pleasant. Al-Dahhak said: "nor pleasant" means nor sweet.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs make karim follow anything from which they negate a quality, intending blame by it. They say: "He is not fat nor karim," and "This house is not spacious nor karimah."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned their deeds for which they deserved punishment, saying: ﴿Indeed they were before that affluent (mutrafin)﴾. This clause gives the reason for what precedes it, meaning: indeed they were, before this punishment that descended upon them, affluent in this world, that is, enjoying what was not lawful for them. Al-mutraf is the one who lives in luxury.

Al-Suddi said: "mushrikin" (polytheists). It has also been said: "mutakabbirin" (arrogant). The first is more apt.

﴿And they used to persist in the great violation﴾. Al-hinth is sin, meaning they persisted in the great sin.

Al-Wahidi said: the people of tafsir said: by it is meant shirk, meaning they did not repent from shirk. This was also the view of al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: it is the great sin from which they did not repent.

Al-Sha'bi said: it is the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus).

﴿And they used to say: "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers, the earliest?"﴾ The hamza in the two places is for denial and disbelief. This matter has already been discussed in al-Saffat and in surah al-Ra'd. The meaning is that they denied and considered it unlikely that they would be raised after death when they had become bones and dust. What is meant is that their flesh and skins became dust and their bones became decayed and crumbling. The governing element of the adverbial phrase is what is indicated by "mab'uthun," because what follows an interrogative does not govern what precedes it. That is: shall we be raised when we die? and so on.

﴿Or our forefathers, the earliest?﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿mab'uthun﴾, because the separation between them is by the hamza. The meaning is that the resurrection of their earliest forefathers is more remote, because their death came earlier. It is also read "wa-aba'una" (with a different reading).

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to answer them and to reject their disbelief, saying: ﴿Say: "Indeed the earliest and the latest﴾ ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day﴾." That is: say to them, O Muhammad, that indeed the earliest of the nations and the latest of them, of whom you are part, will surely be gathered after the resurrection ﴿to the appointed time of a known day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers﴾. This and what follows are part of what falls under the saying, and it is conjoined to "indeed the earliest." He, glorified is He, described them with two ugly attributes: straying from the truth, and denying it.

﴿You will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum﴾, meaning: you will surely eat in the Hereafter from a tree whose appearance is hateful and whose taste is hateful. Its tafsir has already been given in surah al-Saffat. The first min is for the beginning of the limit, and the second is explanatory. It is also permissible that the first min is superfluous and the second is explanatory, or that the second is superfluous and the first is for the beginning.

﴿And filling your bellies with it﴾, meaning you will fill your bellies with the tree of zaqqum because of the severe hunger that will befall you.

﴿Then you will drink on top of it from the boiling water﴾. The pronoun in "on it" refers to the zaqqum, and hamim is water whose heat has reached its extreme. The meaning is: you will drink on top of the zaqqum, immediately after eating it, from scalding water. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to "tree," because it can be masculine or feminine. It is also possible that it refers to the eating that is indicated by His saying "you will surely eat." It has been read "min shajarah" (from a tree) in the singular.

﴿So you will drink as thirsty camels drink (shurb al-him)﴾. Al-Jumhur read "shurb al-him" with a fatha on the shin. Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah read it with a damma, and Mujahid and Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi read it with a kasra. These are dialects. Abu Zayd said: I heard the Arabs say it with a damma on the shin, a fatha, and a kasra. Al-Mubarrad said: the fatha is on the basis of the verbal noun (masdar), and the damma is the noun of the verbal noun (ism al-masdar). Al-him are thirsty camels that are not satisfied because of a disease that afflicts them. This clause explains what precedes it: meaning, your drinking will not be ordinary drinking, but like the drinking of al-him, which are thirsty and are not quenched by drinking water. The singular of al-him is ahyam, and the feminine is hayma'.

Qays ibn al-Mulawwah said:
It is said that the disease of love (hiyam) afflicted him, and my soul knew the place of my cure.

Al-Dahhak, Ibn 'Uyaynah, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan said: al-Hiym is the easy land with sand, and the meaning is that they drink as this land drinks water and no trace of it appears in it.

[p-1448] Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: al-Hiyam with a damma is the most intense thirst, and al-hiyam is like madness from love. Al-hiyam is a disease that takes camels so that they wander the land and do not graze. One says a she-camel is hayma'. Al-hayma' is also the desert with no water in it. Al-hiyam with a fatha is sand that does not hold together in the hand because of its softness, and its plural is huyum like qadhal and qudhul. Al-hiyam with a kasra is thirsty camels.

﴿This is their hospitality on the Day of Judgment﴾. Al-Jumhur read "nuzuluhum" with two dammas. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Muhaysin with one damma and a sukun. It has already been mentioned that al-nuzul is what is prepared for a guest and is the first thing he eats. The Day of Judgment is the Day of Recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that what has been mentioned of the tree of zaqqum and the drink of boiling water is what is prepared for them, and what they eat on the Day of Resurrection. In this there is mockery of them, because nuzul is what is prepared for guests as an honour for them. A similar example is His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 56, verses 27–56 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Hakim, who declared it sound (ṣaḥīḥ), and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "Allah benefits us through the Bedouins and their questions." "A Bedouin came one day and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, a harmful tree is mentioned in the Qur'an, and I did not think there was a tree in Paradise that harms its companion.' He said: 'And what is it?' He said: 'The lote tree (sidr), for it has thorns.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Did Allah not say: ﴿Among thornless lote trees﴾? Allah will remove its thorns and place in the stead of each thorn a fruit, and it will bring forth fruit which splits open to reveal seventy-two kinds of food, no two of which resemble each other.'"

Ibn Abi Dawud, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿUyaynah ibn ʿAbd al-Sulami, who said: "I was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) when a Bedouin came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I hear you mention a tree in Paradise, and I know of no tree with more thorns than it—meaning the acacia (ṭalḥ).' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah will place in the stead of each of its thorns a fruit like the testicle of a castrated ram, and in it there will be seventy kinds of food, no one of which resembles another.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿among thornless lote trees﴾ that he said: "He removed its thorns and made it heavy with fruit."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through several chains from him (Ibn ʿAbbas), who said: "The makhdud is that which has no thorn in it."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd also narrated from him: "The makhdud is the laden one that has no thorn in it."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib regarding His words ﴿and acacia laden with fruit﴾ that he said: "It is the banana (mawz)."

al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Hurayrah the same.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri the same.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib that he recited ﴿and banana (ṭalʿ) laden with fruit﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from Qays ibn ʿUbbad, who said: "I recited to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib '﴿and acacia laden with fruit﴾,' and ʿAli said: 'What is the matter with the acacia? Do you not recite ﴿and banana (ṭalʿ)﴾?' Then he said: ﴿banana arranged in tiers﴾ [Qaf 50:10]. It was said to him: 'O Commander of the Faithful, shall we erase it from the Mushaf?' He said: 'The Qur'an is not to be stirred up today.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿arranged in tiers﴾ that he said: "Some of it is upon others."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Indeed in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider can travel for a hundred years without crossing it. Recite if you wish: ﴿and extended shade﴾."

al-Bukhari and others narrated something similar from the hadith of Anas.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated something similar from the hadith of Abu Saʿid.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), al-Nasai, and others narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His words ﴿and raised couches﴾ that he said: "Their height is as the distance between the heaven and the earth, and the journey between them is five hundred years."

After narrating it, al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib (strange) hadith, which we do not know except from the narration of Rishdin ibn Saʿd." And Rishdin is weak (ḍaʿīf).

al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His words ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special production﴾: 'The produced ones are those who were in the world, old women, blear-eyed and with discharge.'"

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: "It is gharib, and Musa and Yazid are weak."

al-Tayalisi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Qani', and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth narrated from Salamah ibn Yazid al-Juʿfi, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say regarding His words ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special production﴾: 'They are the previously married and the virgins who were in the world.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "He created them other than their first creation."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿virgins﴾ that he said: "Maidens."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth narrated through the chain of ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿loving, of equal age﴾ that he said: "Loving: ʿawashiq (passionate toward their husbands)." And regarding "equal age" he said: "Equal in age, meaning equal."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿loving﴾ that he said: "Passionate toward their husbands, and their husbands are passionate toward them." Regarding "equal age" he said: "At one age, thirty-three years."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also that he said: "The ʿarub is the one who is coquettish toward her husband."

Musaddad in his Musnad (a collection arranged by companion), Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a fair chain (ḥasan) from Abu Bakrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His words ﴿a multitude from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a multitude from the later ones﴾ that he said: "Both of them are from this Ummah."

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Musaddad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakrah regarding His words ﴿a multitude from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a multitude from the later ones﴾ that he said: "They are both from this Ummah."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn ʿAdi, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said with a weak chain, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿a multitude from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a multitude from the later ones﴾ that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Both of them are from my Ummah.'"

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The two multitudes together are from this Ummah."

al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, narrated from Ibn (p-1449) ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾ that he said: "Of black smoke," and in another wording: "Of the smoke of Hell."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿drinking like thirsty camels﴾ that he said: "The thirsty camels."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 56, verses 27–56 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glorified is He, finished mentioning the states of the foremost (al-sabiqun) and what He had prepared for them of lasting bliss, He mentioned the states of the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand: what of the companions of the right hand?﴾ We have already explained the grammatical construction (i'rab) of this statement, and the magnification and exaltation contained in this interrogative clause. It is the predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada'), which is "companions of the right hand."

His saying: ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns﴾ is a second predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are among lote-trees without thorns. Al-sidr is a kind of tree, and al-makhdud is that whose thorns have been removed, meaning cut off, so that there are no thorns on it.

Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said, describing Paradise:
Indeed the gardens in the Gardens are shady, in them are the maidens, and their lote-trees are thornless.

Al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: indeed al-sidr al-makhdud is that which is laden with fruit (al-mawqur hamlan).

﴿And acacia arranged in tiers﴾. Most of the exegetes said that al-talh in the verse is the banana tree (shajar al-mawz).

A group said: it is not the banana tree, but the well-known talh, which is the greatest of the trees of the Arabs.

Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is a large tree that has thorns.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-talh is Umm Ghaylan, and it has a pleasant blossom. So they were addressed and promised what they love, except that its excellence over what is in this world is like the excellence of all that is in Paradise over what is in this world.

He said: it is possible that it is in Paradise but its thorns have been removed.

Al-Suddi said: the acacia of Paradise resembles the acacia of this world, but it has fruit sweeter than honey. Al-mandud is that which is piled up, whose beginning and end are arranged with fruit, and which has no protruding branches.

Masruq said: the trees of Paradise, from their roots to their branches, are arranged in tiers with fruit entirely; whenever a fruit is taken, another better than it grows in its place.

﴿And spreading shade﴾, meaning lasting and enduring, which does not cease and which the sun does not cancel.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: the Arabs call everything long that does not end "mamdud" (extended). From this is His saying: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shade?﴾ [al-Furqan: 45]. And the whole of Paradise is shade, with no sun in it.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it means the shade of the Throne. From the Arabs' use of "mamdud" for what is enduring and does not end is the saying of Labid:
Grief overcame patience, though I was not one to be overcome; a long-lasting, enduring time.

﴿And water poured out﴾, meaning flowing continuously by night and day wherever they wish, not ceasing for them. It is poured out, which God pours out in its channels. The origin of al-sakb is pouring; one says "sakaba-hu sakban", meaning he poured it.

﴿And fruit abundant﴾, meaning varied kinds, multiplied.

﴿Neither cut off﴾ at any time, as the fruits of this world are cut off at certain times, ﴿nor forbidden﴾, meaning they are not withheld from whoever wishes them at any time or in any condition. Rather, they are prepared for whoever wishes them, and nothing stands between him and them.

Ibn Qutaybah said: it means they are not prohibited to them as the gardens of this world are guarded against.

﴿And raised couches﴾, meaning raised, some of them above others, or raised upon couches.

It has been said that the couches here are a metaphor for the women of Paradise, and their being raised means that they are upon thrones (al-ara'ik), or that they are elevated in rank in beauty and perfection.

﴿Indeed We produced them with a production﴾, meaning We created them with a new creation without procreation. It has also been said that what is meant is the women of the children of Adam, and the meaning is that God, glorified is He, returned them after death to the state of youth. Although the women have not been mentioned before, they have entered among the companions of the right hand. As for the view of the one who said that the raised couches are the women themselves, the reference of the pronoun is clear.

﴿And We made them virgins﴾, ﴿untouched by man or jinn before them﴾.

﴿Loving, of equal age﴾. Ruba is the plural of 'arub, who is the one who is affectionate toward her husband.

Al-Mubarrad said: she is the one who loves her husband, and from this is the saying of Labid:
And in the tent is one who is loving, not indecent, whose buttocks are full, whose light dazzles the sight.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: she is the one good in speech.

Al-Jumhur read it with a damma on the 'ayn and the ra'. Hamzah and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with sukun on the ra', and both are dialects for the plural of fa'ul. Al-atrab are those who are of the same birth and the same age.

Mujahid said: atraban means similar and of the same forms.

Al-Suddi said: atraban in character, with no hatred or envy among them.

His saying: ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾ is connected to "We produced them," or to "We made them," or to "atraban." The meaning is that God produced them for their sake, or created them for their sake, or they are equal to the companions of the right hand in age. Or it is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are for the companions of the right hand.

﴿A company from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿a company from the later ones﴾. This refers back to His saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand: what of the companions of the right hand?﴾, meaning they are a company from the earlier ones and a company from the later ones. The tafsir of thulla has already been given when mentioning the foremost. The meaning is that they are a group, or a community, or a party, or a portion, from the earlier ones, who are from Adam until our Prophet (ﷺ), and a group, or a community, or a party, or a portion, from the later ones, who are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and al-Dahhak said: ﴿A company from the earlier ones﴾ means from the foremost of this community, and ﴿a company from the later ones﴾ means from this community, from its last part.

Then, when He, glorified is He, finished with what He had prepared for the companions of the right hand, He began to mention the companions of the left (ashab al-shimal) and what He had prepared for them, saying: ﴿And the companions of the left hand: what of the companions of the left hand?﴾ The discussion of the grammatical construction of this and of the magnification within it is as was mentioned for the companions of the right hand.

His saying: ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾ is either a second predicate of the companions of the left hand, or the predicate of an omitted subject. Al-samum is the heat of the Fire, and al-hamim is water extremely hot, and its meaning has already been explained.

It has been said that al-samum is the hot wind that enters the pores of the body.

﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾. Al-yahmum is the form yafa'ul from al-ahamm, which is black. The Arabs say "aswad yahmum" when something is intensely black. The meaning is that they resort to shade, but they find it a shade of black smoke from the smoke of Hell.

It has also been said that it is derived from al-hamm, which is fat blackened by the burning of fire.

It has also been said that it is derived from al-humum, which is charcoal.

Al-Dahhak said: the Fire is black and everything in it is black.

Then He described this shade by His saying: ﴿Neither cool nor pleasant﴾, meaning it is not like other shades that are cool, but rather it is hot because it comes from the smoke of the fire of Hell.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "nor pleasant" means it has no pleasant appearance, and everything that has no good in it is not pleasant. Al-Dahhak said: "nor pleasant" means nor sweet.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs make karim follow anything from which they negate a quality, intending blame by it. They say: "He is not fat nor karim," and "This house is not spacious nor karimah."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned their deeds for which they deserved punishment, saying: ﴿Indeed they were before that affluent (mutrafin)﴾. This clause gives the reason for what precedes it, meaning: indeed they were, before this punishment that descended upon them, affluent in this world, that is, enjoying what was not lawful for them. Al-mutraf is the one who lives in luxury.

Al-Suddi said: "mushrikin" (polytheists). It has also been said: "mutakabbirin" (arrogant). The first is more apt.

﴿And they used to persist in the great violation﴾. Al-hinth is sin, meaning they persisted in the great sin.

Al-Wahidi said: the people of tafsir said: by it is meant shirk, meaning they did not repent from shirk. This was also the view of al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: it is the great sin from which they did not repent.

Al-Sha'bi said: it is the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus).

﴿And they used to say: "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers, the earliest?"﴾ The hamza in the two places is for denial and disbelief. This matter has already been discussed in al-Saffat and in surah al-Ra'd. The meaning is that they denied and considered it unlikely that they would be raised after death when they had become bones and dust. What is meant is that their flesh and skins became dust and their bones became decayed and crumbling. The governing element of the adverbial phrase is what is indicated by "mab'uthun," because what follows an interrogative does not govern what precedes it. That is: shall we be raised when we die? and so on.

﴿Or our forefathers, the earliest?﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿mab'uthun﴾, because the separation between them is by the hamza. The meaning is that the resurrection of their earliest forefathers is more remote, because their death came earlier. It is also read "wa-aba'una" (with a different reading).

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to answer them and to reject their disbelief, saying: ﴿Say: "Indeed the earliest and the latest﴾ ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day﴾." That is: say to them, O Muhammad, that indeed the earliest of the nations and the latest of them, of whom you are part, will surely be gathered after the resurrection ﴿to the appointed time of a known day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers﴾. This and what follows are part of what falls under the saying, and it is conjoined to "indeed the earliest." He, glorified is He, described them with two ugly attributes: straying from the truth, and denying it.

﴿You will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum﴾, meaning: you will surely eat in the Hereafter from a tree whose appearance is hateful and whose taste is hateful. Its tafsir has already been given in surah al-Saffat. The first min is for the beginning of the limit, and the second is explanatory. It is also permissible that the first min is superfluous and the second is explanatory, or that the second is superfluous and the first is for the beginning.

﴿And filling your bellies with it﴾, meaning you will fill your bellies with the tree of zaqqum because of the severe hunger that will befall you.

﴿Then you will drink on top of it from the boiling water﴾. The pronoun in "on it" refers to the zaqqum, and hamim is water whose heat has reached its extreme. The meaning is: you will drink on top of the zaqqum, immediately after eating it, from scalding water. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to "tree," because it can be masculine or feminine. It is also possible that it refers to the eating that is indicated by His saying "you will surely eat." It has been read "min shajarah" (from a tree) in the singular.

﴿So you will drink as thirsty camels drink (shurb al-him)﴾. Al-Jumhur read "shurb al-him" with a fatha on the shin. Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah read it with a damma, and Mujahid and Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi read it with a kasra. These are dialects. Abu Zayd said: I heard the Arabs say it with a damma on the shin, a fatha, and a kasra. Al-Mubarrad said: the fatha is on the basis of the verbal noun (masdar), and the damma is the noun of the verbal noun (ism al-masdar). Al-him are thirsty camels that are not satisfied because of a disease that afflicts them. This clause explains what precedes it: meaning, your drinking will not be ordinary drinking, but like the drinking of al-him, which are thirsty and are not quenched by drinking water. The singular of al-him is ahyam, and the feminine is hayma'.

It is said that the disease of love (hiyam) afflicted him, and my soul knew the place of my cure.

Al-Dahhak, Ibn 'Uyaynah, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan said: al-Hiym is the easy land with sand, and the meaning is that they drink as this land drinks water and no trace of it appears in it.

[p-1448] Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: al-Hiyam with a damma is the most intense thirst, and al-hiyam is like madness from love. Al-hiyam is a disease that takes camels so that they wander the land and do not graze. One says a she-camel is hayma'. Al-hayma' is also the desert with no water in it. Al-hiyam with a fatha is sand that does not hold together in the hand because of its softness, and its plural is huyum like qadhal and qudhul. Al-hiyam with a kasra is thirsty camels.

A similar example is His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21].

Al-Hakim, who declared it sound (ṣaḥīḥ), and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "Allah benefits us through the Bedouins and their questions." "A Bedouin came one day and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, a harmful tree is mentioned in the Qur'an, and I did not think there was a tree in Paradise that harms its companion.' He said: 'And what is it?' He said: 'The lote tree (sidr), for it has thorns.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Did Allah not say: ﴿Among thornless lote trees﴾? Allah will remove its thorns and place in the stead of each thorn a fruit, and it will bring forth fruit which splits open to reveal seventy-two kinds of food, no two of which resemble each other.'"

Ibn Abi Dawud, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿUyaynah ibn ʿAbd al-Sulami, who said: "I was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) when a Bedouin came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I hear you mention a tree in Paradise, and I know of no tree with more thorns than it—meaning the acacia (ṭalḥ).' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah will place in the stead of each of its thorns a fruit like the testicle of a castrated ram, and in it there will be seventy kinds of food, no one of which resembles another.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿among thornless lote trees﴾ that he said: "He removed its thorns and made it heavy with fruit."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through several chains from him (Ibn ʿAbbas), who said: "The makhdud is that which has no thorn in it."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd also narrated from him: "The makhdud is the laden one that has no thorn in it."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib regarding His words ﴿and acacia laden with fruit﴾ that he said: "It is the banana (mawz)."

al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Hurayrah the same.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri the same.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib that he recited ﴿and banana (ṭalʿ) laden with fruit﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from Qays ibn ʿUbbad, who said: "I recited to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib '﴿and acacia laden with fruit﴾,' and ʿAli said: 'What is the matter with the acacia? Do you not recite ﴿and banana (ṭalʿ)﴾?' Then he said: ﴿banana arranged in tiers﴾ [Qaf 50:10]. It was said to him: 'O Commander of the Faithful, shall we erase it from the Mushaf?' He said: 'The Qur'an is not to be stirred up today.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿arranged in tiers﴾ that he said: "Some of it is upon others."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Indeed in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider can travel for a hundred years without crossing it. Recite if you wish: ﴿and extended shade﴾."

al-Bukhari and others narrated something similar from the hadith of Anas.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated something similar from the hadith of Abu Saʿid.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), al-Nasai, and others narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His words ﴿and raised couches﴾ that he said: "Their height is as the distance between the heaven and the earth, and the journey between them is five hundred years."

After narrating it, al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib (strange) hadith, which we do not know except from the narration of Rishdin ibn Saʿd." And Rishdin is weak (ḍaʿīf).

al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His words ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special production﴾: 'The produced ones are those who were in the world, old women, blear-eyed and with discharge.'"

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: "It is gharib, and Musa and Yazid are weak."

al-Tayalisi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Qani', and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth narrated from Salamah ibn Yazid al-Juʿfi, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say regarding His words ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special production﴾: 'They are the previously married and the virgins who were in the world.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "He created them other than their first creation."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿virgins﴾ that he said: "Maidens."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Baʿth narrated through the chain of ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿loving, of equal age﴾ that he said: "Loving: ʿawashiq (passionate toward their husbands)." And regarding "equal age" he said: "Equal in age, meaning equal."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿loving﴾ that he said: "Passionate toward their husbands, and their husbands are passionate toward them." Regarding "equal age" he said: "At one age, thirty-three years."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also that he said: "The ʿarub is the one who is coquettish toward her husband."

Musaddad in his Musnad (a collection arranged by companion), Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a fair chain (ḥasan) from Abu Bakrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His words ﴿a multitude from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a multitude from the later ones﴾ that he said: "Both of them are from this Ummah."

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Musaddad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakrah regarding His words ﴿a multitude from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a multitude from the later ones﴾ that he said: "They are both from this Ummah."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn ʿAdi, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said with a weak chain, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿a multitude from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a multitude from the later ones﴾ that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Both of them are from my Ummah.'"

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The two multitudes together are from this Ummah."

al-Firyabi, Saʿid ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, narrated from Ibn (p-1449) ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾ that he said: "Of black smoke," and in another wording: "Of the smoke of Hell."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿drinking like thirsty camels﴾ that he said: "The thirsty camels."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 56, verses 27–56 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glorified is He, finished mentioning the states of the foremost (al-sabiqun) and what He had prepared for them of lasting bliss, He mentioned the states of the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand: what of the companions of the right hand?﴾ We have already explained the grammatical construction (i'rab) of this statement, and the magnification and exaltation contained in this interrogative clause. It is the predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada'), which is "companions of the right hand."

His saying: ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns﴾ is a second predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are among lote-trees without thorns. Al-sidr is a kind of tree, and al-makhdud is that whose thorns have been removed, meaning cut off, so that there are no thorns on it.

Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said, describing Paradise:
Indeed the gardens in the Gardens are shady, in them are the maidens, and their lote-trees are thornless.

Al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: indeed al-sidr al-makhdud is that which is laden with fruit (al-mawqur hamlan).

﴿And acacia arranged in tiers﴾. Most of the exegetes said that al-talh in the verse is the banana tree (shajar al-mawz).

A group said: it is not the banana tree, but the well-known talh, which is the greatest of the trees of the Arabs.

Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is a large tree that has thorns.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-talh is Umm Ghaylan, and it has a pleasant blossom. So they were addressed and promised what they love, except that its excellence over what is in this world is like the excellence of all that is in Paradise over what is in this world.

He said: it is possible that it is in Paradise but its thorns have been removed.

Al-Suddi said: the acacia of Paradise resembles the acacia of this world, but it has fruit sweeter than honey. Al-mandud is that which is piled up, whose beginning and end are arranged with fruit, and which has no protruding branches.

Masruq said: the trees of Paradise, from their roots to their branches, are arranged in tiers with fruit entirely; whenever a fruit is taken, another better than it grows in its place.

﴿And spreading shade﴾, meaning lasting and enduring, which does not cease and which the sun does not cancel.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: the Arabs call everything long that does not end "mamdud" (extended). From this is His saying: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shade?﴾ [al-Furqan: 45]. And the whole of Paradise is shade, with no sun in it.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it means the shade of the Throne. From the Arabs' use of "mamdud" for what is enduring and does not end is the saying of Labid:
Grief overcame patience, though I was not one to be overcome; a long-lasting, enduring time.

﴿And water poured out﴾, meaning flowing continuously by night and day wherever they wish, not ceasing for them. It is poured out, which God pours out in its channels. The origin of al-sakb is pouring; one says "sakaba-hu sakban", meaning he poured it.

﴿And fruit abundant﴾, meaning varied kinds, multiplied.

﴿Neither cut off﴾ at any time, as the fruits of this world are cut off at certain times, ﴿nor forbidden﴾, meaning they are not withheld from whoever wishes them at any time or in any condition. Rather, they are prepared for whoever wishes them, and nothing stands between him and them.

Ibn Qutaybah said: it means they are not prohibited to them as the gardens of this world are guarded against.

﴿And raised couches﴾, meaning raised, some of them above others, or raised upon couches.

It has been said that the couches here are a metaphor for the women of Paradise, and their being raised means that they are upon thrones (al-ara'ik), or that they are elevated in rank in beauty and perfection.

﴿Indeed We produced them with a production﴾, meaning We created them with a new creation without procreation. It has also been said that what is meant is the women of the children of Adam, and the meaning is that God, glorified is He, returned them after death to the state of youth. Although the women have not been mentioned before, they have entered among the companions of the right hand. As for the view of the one who said that the raised couches are the women themselves, the reference of the pronoun is clear.

﴿And We made them virgins﴾, ﴿untouched by man or jinn before them﴾.

﴿Loving, of equal age﴾. Ruba is the plural of 'arub, who is the one who is affectionate toward her husband.

Al-Mubarrad said: she is the one who loves her husband, and from this is the saying of Labid:
And in the tent is one who is loving, not indecent, whose buttocks are full, whose light dazzles the sight.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: she is the one good in speech.

Al-Jumhur read it with a damma on the 'ayn and the ra'. Hamzah and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with sukun on the ra', and both are dialects for the plural of fa'ul. Al-atrab are those who are of the same birth and the same age.

Mujahid said: atraban means similar and of the same forms.

Al-Suddi said: atraban in character, with no hatred or envy among them.

His saying: ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾ is connected to "We produced them," or to "We made them," or to "atraban." The meaning is that God produced them for their sake, or created them for their sake, or they are equal to the companions of the right hand in age. Or it is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are for the companions of the right hand.

﴿A company from the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿a company from the later ones﴾. This refers back to His saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand: what of the companions of the right hand?﴾, meaning they are a company from the earlier ones and a company from the later ones. The tafsir of thulla has already been given when mentioning the foremost. The meaning is that they are a group, or a community, or a party, or a portion, from the earlier ones, who are from Adam until our Prophet (ﷺ), and a group, or a community, or a party, or a portion, from the later ones, who are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and al-Dahhak said: ﴿A company from the earlier ones﴾ means from the foremost of this community, and ﴿a company from the later ones﴾ means from this community, from its last part.

Then, when He, glorified is He, finished with what He had prepared for the companions of the right hand, He began to mention the companions of the left (ashab al-shimal) and what He had prepared for them, saying: ﴿And the companions of the left hand: what of the companions of the left hand?﴾ The discussion of the grammatical construction of this and of the magnification within it is as was mentioned for the companions of the right hand.

His saying: ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾ is either a second predicate of the companions of the left hand, or the predicate of an omitted subject. Al-samum is the heat of the Fire, and al-hamim is water extremely hot, and its meaning has already been explained.

It has been said that al-samum is the hot wind that enters the pores of the body.

﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾. Al-yahmum is the form yafa'ul from al-ahamm, which is black. The Arabs say "aswad yahmum" when something is intensely black. The meaning is that they resort to shade, but they find it a shade of black smoke from the smoke of Hell.

It has also been said that it is derived from al-hamm, which is fat blackened by the burning of fire.

It has also been said that it is derived from al-humum, which is charcoal.

Al-Dahhak said: the Fire is black and everything in it is black.

Then He described this shade by His saying: ﴿Neither cool nor pleasant﴾, meaning it is not like other shades that are cool, but rather it is hot because it comes from the smoke of the fire of Hell.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "nor pleasant" means it has no pleasant appearance, and everything that has no good in it is not pleasant. Al-Dahhak said: "nor pleasant" means nor sweet.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs make karim follow anything from which they negate a quality, intending blame by it. They say: "He is not fat nor karim," and "This house is not spacious nor karimah."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned their deeds for which they deserved punishment, saying: ﴿Indeed they were before that affluent (mutrafin)﴾. This clause gives the reason for what precedes it, meaning: indeed they were, before this punishment that descended upon them, affluent in this world, that is, enjoying what was not lawful for them. Al-mutraf is the one who lives in luxury.

Al-Suddi said: "mushrikin" (polytheists). It has also been said: "mutakabbirin" (arrogant). The first is more apt.

﴿And they used to persist in the great violation﴾. Al-hinth is sin, meaning they persisted in the great sin.

Al-Wahidi said: the people of tafsir said: by it is meant shirk, meaning they did not repent from shirk. This was also the view of al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: it is the great sin from which they did not repent.

Al-Sha'bi said: it is the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus).

﴿And they used to say: "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers, the earliest?"﴾ The hamza in the two places is for denial and disbelief. This matter has already been discussed in al-Saffat and in surah al-Ra'd. The meaning is that they denied and considered it unlikely that they would be raised after death when they had become bones and dust. What is meant is that their flesh and skins became dust and their bones became decayed and crumbling. The governing element of the adverbial phrase is what is indicated by "mab'uthun," because what follows an interrogative does not govern what precedes it. That is: shall we be raised when we die? and so on.

﴿Or our forefathers, the earliest?﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun in ﴿mab'uthun﴾, because the separation between them is by the hamza. The meaning is that the resurrection of their earliest forefathers is more remote, because their death came earlier. It is also read "wa-aba'una" (with a different reading).

Then God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to answer them and to reject their disbelief, saying: ﴿Say: "Indeed the earliest and the latest﴾ ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day﴾." That is: say to them, O Muhammad, that indeed the earliest of the nations and the latest of them, of whom you are part, will surely be gathered after the resurrection ﴿to the appointed time of a known day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers﴾. This and what follows are part of what falls under the saying, and it is conjoined to "indeed the earliest." He, glorified is He, described them with two ugly attributes: straying from the truth, and denying it.

﴿You will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum﴾, meaning: you will surely eat in the Hereafter from a tree whose appearance is hateful and whose taste is hateful. Its tafsir has already been given in surah al-Saffat. The first min is for the beginning of the limit, and the second is explanatory. It is also permissible that the first min is superfluous and the second is explanatory, or that the second is superfluous and the first is for the beginning.

﴿And filling your bellies with it﴾, meaning you will fill your bellies with the tree of zaqqum because of the severe hunger that will befall you.

﴿Then you will drink on top of it from the boiling water﴾. The pronoun in "on it" refers to the zaqqum, and hamim is water whose heat has reached its extreme. The meaning is: you will drink on top of the zaqqum, immediately after eating it, from scalding water. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to "tree," because it can be masculine or feminine. It is also possible that it refers to the eating that is indicated by His saying "you will surely eat." It has been read "min shajarah" (from a tree) in the singular.

﴿So you will drink as thirsty camels drink (shurb al-him)﴾. Al-Jumhur read "shurb al-him" with a fatha on the shin. Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah read it with a damma, and Mujahid and Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi read it with a kasra. These are dialects. Abu Zayd said: I heard the Arabs say it with a damma on the shin, a fatha, and a kasra. Al-Mubarrad said: the fatha is on the basis of the verbal noun (masdar), and the damma is the noun of the verbal noun (ism al-masdar). Al-him are thirsty camels that are not satisfied because of a disease that afflicts them. This clause explains what precedes it: meaning, your drinking will not be ordinary drinking, but like the drinking of al-him, which are thirsty and are not quenched by drinking water. The singular of al-him is ahyam, and the feminine is hayma'.

Qays ibn al-Mulawwah said:
It is said that the disease of love (hiyam) afflicted him, and my soul knew the place of my cure.

Al-Dahhak, Ibn 'Uyaynah, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan said: al-Hiym is the easy land with sand, and the meaning is that they drink as this land drinks water and no trace of it appears in it.

[p-1448] Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: al-Hiyam with a damma is the most intense thirst, and al-hiyam is like madness from love. Al-hiyam is a disease that takes camels so that they wander the land and do not graze. One says a she-camel is hayma'. Al-hayma' is also the desert with no water in it. Al-hiyam with a fatha is sand that does not hold together in the hand because of its softness, and its plural is huyum like qadhal and qudhul. Al-hiyam with a kasra is thirsty camels.

﴿This is their hospitality on the Day of Judgment﴾. Al-Jumhur read "nuzuluhum" with two dammas. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr and Ibn Muhaysin with one damma and a sukun. It has already been mentioned that al-nuzul is what is prepared for a guest and is the first thing he eats. The Day of Judgment is the Day of Recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that what has been mentioned of the tree of zaqqum and the drink of boiling water is what is prepared for them, and what they eat on the Day of Resurrection. In this there is mockery of them, because nuzul is what is prepared for guests as an honour for them. A similar example is His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 56, verses 27–56 (part 2 of 2):

"A Bedouin came one day and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, a harmful tree is mentioned in the Qur'an, and I did not think there was a tree in Paradise that harms its companion.' He said: 'And what is it?' He said: 'The lote tree (sidr), for it has thorns.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Did Allah not say: ﴿Among thornless lote trees﴾?
