According to this dialect, there is no omitted genitive in the verse, rather the meaning of *rizq* (provision) is thanks. The reason for expressing thanks by *rizq* is that thanks overflows with an increase of provision, so thanks becomes a provision, expressing the cause by the effect (*taʿbīr bil-sabab ʿan al-musabbab*). Among what falls under this verse is the saying of the disbelievers when Allah gives them drink and sends rain down upon them: "We were given drink by such-and-such a star, and we were given rain by such-and-such a star."

al-Azharī said: the meaning of the verse is: instead of thanking Him, you make your provision, which Allah has provided you, the denial that it is from Allah the Provider.

ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās recited *wa-tajʿalūna shukrakum* ("and you make your thanks"). The majority recited ﴿annakum tukadhdhibūn﴾ with a doubled *dhāl* from *al-takdhīb* (denial), while ʿAlī and ʿĀṣim, in one narration from him, recited it with a light *dhāl* from *al-kadhib* (lying).

﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat﴾, meaning: then why not, when the soul or the self reaches the throat at death. No reference to it has preceded, because the meaning is understood by them when they use such an expression. From this is the saying of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī:

"O Māwiyyah, wealth does not avail a man when the death-rattle takes him one day and the chest constricts upon it."

﴿And you at that moment are looking on﴾, at what he is in, that one whose soul or spirit has reached the throat.

al-Zajjāj said: "And you, O people of the dead, in that state, see the dead one as he has come to the point of his soul leaving. The meaning is that in that state they cannot repel it from him, and they cannot do anything that benefits him or lightens what he is in."

﴿And We are nearer to him than you﴾, meaning by knowledge, power and sight. It was said: He meant that Our messengers, who take charge of seizing him, are nearer to him than you. ﴿But you do not perceive﴾, meaning you do not comprehend that, due to your ignorance that Allah is nearer to His servant than his jugular vein. Or: you do not see the angels of death who attend the dead one and take charge of seizing him.

﴿Then why, if you are not to be judged﴾ ﴿you do not return it?﴾ It is said: *dāna al-sulṭānu raʿiyyatahu*, when the ruler governed his subjects and enslaved them. Al-Farrāʾ said: *dintuhu*: I possessed him. He recited for al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"You have indeed governed the affairs of your sons, until you left them finer than flour."

That is, you possessed them. It is also said *dānahu* means he humbled him and enslaved him. It was said the meaning of *madīnīna* is those called to account (*muḥāsabūn*), and it was said: those who will be recompensed (*majziyyūn*), and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Nothing remains but the enemies; we have repaid them as they repaid."

The first meaning is closer to the sense of the verse, that is: then why, if you are not those who are ruled and owned, do you not return it, namely the soul which has reached the throat, to its place where it was? ﴿If you are truthful﴾, and you will not return it, so your claim that you are not ruled nor owned is refuted. The operator of *idhā balaghat* ("when it reaches") is *turjiʿūnahā* ("you return it"), and the second *lawlā* is an emphasis for the first. al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs sometimes repeat the two particles while their meaning is one.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the classes of creation at death and after it, saying: ﴿As for if he is of those brought near﴾, meaning the foremost among the three categories whose details have preceded. ﴿Then rest and provision and a Garden of bliss﴾. Most recited *rawḥun* with a fatḥah on the *rāʾ*, and its meaning is rest from worldly life and relief from their conditions. al-Ḥasan said: *al-rawḥ* is mercy. Mujāhid said: *al-rawḥ* is joy. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, and al-Jaḥdarī recited *fa-rūḥun* with a ḍammah on the *rāʾ*, and this recitation is related from Yaʿqūb, and it is said also from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Muqātil. Muqātil said: it is *al-rizq* (provision) in the dialect of Ḥimyar; one says: "I went out seeking *rayḥān Allāh*," meaning His provision. From this is the saying of al-Namir ibn Tawlab:

"The peace of God and His *rayḥān*, and His mercy, and abundant rain."

Qatādah said: it is the Garden. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is mercy. al-Ḥasan said: it is the well-known *rayḥān* that is smelled. Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: this is at death, and the Garden is kept hidden for him until he is resurrected. Abū al-Jawzāʾ and Abū al-ʿĀliyah said likewise. The meaning of "and a Garden of bliss" is that it is full of luxury. The *rawḥ* and what follows it are in the nominative as the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and the predicate is omitted, meaning: then for him is rest.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 56, verses 75–96 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And as for if he was﴾ that deceased person ﴿one of the companions of the right﴾, and their conditions and the reward Allah has prepared for them have already been mentioned and detailed, ﴿then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾. That is: you will not see among them except what you love of safety, so do not be concerned for them, for they will be safe from the punishment of Allah. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Peace be upon you from them," that is, you are free from distress over them. It has been said that the meaning is: they pray for you and greet you with peace. It has been said that he (ﷺ) is greeted with peace out of honour. It has been said that it is a report from Allah, glorified is He, that some of them greet others with peace. It has been said that the meaning is: "Peace be upon you, O companion of the right, from your brethren, the companions of the right."

﴿And as for if he was one of the deniers, the astray﴾, that is, the deniers of the Resurrection, those who went astray from guidance, and they are the companions of the left, whose mention has preceded and whose conditions have been detailed, ﴿then there is a welcome of boiling water﴾, that is: for him there is a welcome prepared for his arrival, of boiling water (*hamim*), which is water whose heat has reached its extreme. This is after he has eaten from the *zaqqum* as its explanation has preceded.

﴿And the burning of the Hellfire﴾. It is said *aslahu al-nar* and *sallahu*, meaning: when he is placed into the Fire. This is an *idafa* (genitive construction) of the verbal noun to the object, or to the place.

Al-Mubarrad said: The response (*jawab*) of the conditional particle in these three places is omitted, and the estimate is: "Whatever may be the case, then there is rest, etc."

Al-Akhfash said: the *fa'* (the particle *fa*) in the three places is the response of *amma* and the response of the conditional particle together.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿wa-tasliyatu﴾ in the nominative, coordinated upon "fanuzulun" (*fa-nuzulun*). Abu 'Amr, in one of the transmissions from him, read it in the genitive, coordinated upon "hamim" (*min hamim*): that is, "then a welcome of boiling water and of the burning of the Hellfire."

﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty﴾. The reference is to what has been mentioned in this surah, or to what was mentioned shortly before of the conditions of the three groups. It is the true certainty, that is: its pure and unmixed essence. The *idafa* of *haqq* (truth) to *yaqin* (certainty) is of the type of attributing a thing to itself.

Al-Mubarrad said: it is like your saying "*'ayn al-yaqin*" (the eye of certainty) and "*mahd al-yaqin*" (the pure certainty). This is according to the Kufans, and they permitted it because of the difference of wording. As for the Basrans, they hold that the second term of the *idafa* is omitted, and the estimate is: "the true matter of certainty" or "the true report of certainty."

The *fa'* in ﴿so glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it: that is, declare Him free of what does not befit His majesty. The *ba'* (the preposition *bi*) is connected to an omitted element: that is, "so glorify, being associated with the name of your Lord," for blessing through it.

It has been said that the meaning is: "so pray, mentioning your Lord." It has been said that the *ba'* is superfluous, and *al-ism* (the name) means the essence.

It has been said that it indicates transitivity, because *sabbih* (glorify) is transitive by itself at times and transitive by a preposition at other times, and the first is preferable.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* (*Shu'ab al-Iman*) transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Qur'an was sent down in the Night of Decree (*Laylat al-Qadr*) from the highest heaven to the lowest heaven all at once, and then it was revealed in portions over the years." In another wording: "Then it descended from the lowest heaven to the earth in stars (*nujum*)." Then he recited: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him regarding ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ that he said: "The Qur'an." ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾, he said: "The Qur'an."

Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him regarding the verse: "The stars of the Qur'an, when it descends."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ma'rifa* transmitted from several chains from Ibn 'Abbas also regarding ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾ that he said: "The Book that is sent down in the heaven, none touches it but the angels."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Anas regarding ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾ that he said: "The angels."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Alqama, who said: "We came to Salman al-Farisi, and he came out to us from a *kanif* (latrine). We said to him: 'If only you had performed ablution, O Abu 'Abd Allah, and then recited to us such-and-such a surah.' He said: 'Allah only said ﴿in a Book well-protected﴾ ﴿none touches it but the purified﴾, and it is the one that is in the heaven, none touches it but the angels.' Then he recited to us from the Qur'an whatever we wished."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Dawud, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, from his father, who said: "In the letter of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'Amr ibn Hazm: 'None should touch the Qur'an except in a state of purity.'"

Malik transmitted it in *al-Muwatta'* from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr.

Abu Dawud transmitted it in *al-Marasil* (the collection of *mursal* reports) from the hadith of al-Zuhri, who said: "He read in the manuscript of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'None who is not pure should touch the Qur'an.'" Al-Daraqutni traced it back to 'Amr ibn Hazm, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, and 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, but there is scrutiny regarding their chains.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Umar that he would not touch the *mushaf* (the codex) except when in a state of ablution.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba in *al-Musannaf*, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, who said: "We were with Salman, and he set off for a need, then he hid from us, then came out to us. We said: 'If only you had performed ablution, so we could ask you about some matters of the Qur'an.' He said: 'Ask me, for I will not touch it; only the purified touch it.' Then he recited ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None who is not pure should touch the Qur'an." Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that when the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to Yemen, he wrote for him in his instructions: "That none who is not pure should touch the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Do you then disbelieve/ are you [of those who] deny?﴾ (*mudhinun*) that he said: "Deniers (*mukadhdhibun*)."

Muslim, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The people were given rain during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'In the morning some of the people are thankful and some of them are disbelievers. They said: "This is a mercy that Allah has placed." And some of them said: "Such-and-such a *nawʾ* (star-rising) has indeed brought it." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ until ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾'" The essence of the hadith, without mention that it is the cause of the revelation of the verse, is established in the two *Sahihs* from the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani and from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

There are other hadiths on this subject.

Ahmad, Ibn Mani', 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it *hasan*), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtara* transmitted from 'Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾ that he said: "Your thanks (*shukrakum*). You say: 'We were given rain by such-and-such a *nawʾ* and by such-and-such a star.'"

Ibn 'Asakir in his *Tarikh* transmitted from 'A'isha who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not explain from the Qur'an except a few easy verses."

Regarding His saying ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾, he said: "Your thanks."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Ali that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited '*wa-taj'alna shukrakum*' (and you make your thanks)."

Abu 'Ubayd in *Fada'il al-Qur'an*, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to read "*wa-taj'alna shukrakum*" and said: "He means the star-risings (*al-anwa'*). No people were given rain except that some of them became disbelievers. They used to say: 'We were given rain by such-and-such a star-rising.' So Allah revealed ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from 'Ali, that he read "*wa-taj'alna shukrakum*" and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reading it in this way."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿not subject to judgement (*ghayra madinin*)﴾ that he said: "Not held to account."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* (*Kitab al-Zuhd*), 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym regarding ﴿And as for if he was one of those brought near﴾ — the verse — that he said: "This is for him at death. ﴿And a garden of delight﴾: the Garden is kept hidden for him until the Day he is resurrected. ﴿And as for if he was one of the deniers, the astray﴾ ﴿then there is a welcome of boiling water﴾," he said: "This is at death. ﴿And the burning of the Hellfire﴾," he said: "The Hellfire is kept hidden for him until the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿then rest﴾ that he said: "Fragrance (*ra'iha*)." ﴿And sweet basil (*rayhan*)﴾, he said: "Relief (*istirahah*)."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: "By *al-rayhan* is meant one who is relieved from this world." ﴿And a garden of delight﴾ — he says: "Forgiveness and mercy."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also that he said: "*Al-rayhan* is provision (*al-rizq*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also regarding His saying ﴿Then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾ that he said: "The angels come to him with peace from Allah; they greet him and inform him that he is of the companions of the right."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: ﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty﴾, he said: "What We have related to you in this surah."

He transmitted from him also: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, he said: "Pray to your Lord."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir al-Juhani, who said: "When ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: 'Make it in your *ruku'* (bowing).' Then when ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed, he said: 'Make it in your *sujud* (prostration).'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 56, verses 75–96 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿So I swear not﴾. The majority of the exegetes held that "lā" (لا) is superfluous, for emphasis, and the meaning is "so I swear." This is supported by His later saying, ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you knew﴾. A group of exegetes said that it is for negation, and that what is negated by it is omitted, namely the speech of the disbelieving deniers. Al-Farrā' said: "It is a negation, and the meaning is: the matter is not as you say. Then he began anew and said: 'I swear.'" This was deemed weak, because omitting the subject and predicate of "lā" is not permissible, as Abū Ḥayyān and others said.

It was also said that it is the *lām al-ibtidā'* (the emphatic lām), and the original is *fa-la-uqsimu*, with the fatḥah lengthened so that an alif was produced from it, as in the words of the poet: "I seek refuge in God from the scorpion." Al-Ḥasan, Ḥumayd and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited it thus, *fa-la-uqsimu*, without an alif. According to this view and this recitation (*qirāʾah*), an omitted subject is assumed, and the estimate is: "So as for me, I swear by that."

It was also said that "lā" here has the meaning of "*alā*," the one used for alerting, but this is far-fetched.

It was said that "lā" here is in its literal sense, and that it negates the oath, meaning: "So I do not swear upon this, because the matter is clearer than that." This is rejected by His saying, ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you knew﴾, together with the specification of what is sworn by and what is sworn to.

The meaning of His saying ﴿the setting-places of the stars﴾ is their *masāqiṭ* (places of setting), which are their western points, as Qatādah and others said. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: their *manāzil* (mansions). Al-Ḥasan said: their dispersal and scattering on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they are the *anwāʾ* (star-risings) that the people of the Jāhiliyyah used to say, "We were given rain by the *nawʾ* of such-and-such."

It was also said that the intended meaning of "the setting-places of the stars" is the descent of the Qur'an in parts (*nujūman*) from the *al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ* (the Preserved Tablet). Al-Suddī and others said this. Al-Farrā' related from Ibn Masʿūd that the setting-places of the stars are the *muḥkam* (clear, decisive verses) of the Qur'an.

The majority recited *mawāqiʿi* in the plural, while Ibn Masʿūd, al-Nakhaʿī, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Warsh from Yaʿqūb recited *bi-mawqiʿi* in the singular. Al-Mubarrad said: "*Mawqiʿ* here is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), so it may be singular or plural."

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of the magnification and exaltation of this oath, saying: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you knew﴾. This sentence is a parenthetical clause (*muʿtaraḍah*) between the thing sworn by and the thing sworn to. His saying ﴿if you knew﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the two parts of the parenthetical clause, so it is a parenthesis within a parenthesis.

Al-Farrā' and al-Zajjāj said: "This indicates that the intended meaning of the setting-places of the stars is the descent of the Qur'an. The pronoun in *innahu* refers to the oath implied by *uqsimu* (I swear). The meaning is: indeed the oath by the setting-places of the stars is a mighty oath, if you knew."

Then He mentioned the thing sworn to, saying: ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, meaning: Allah honoured it, made it mighty, and raised its status above all the Books. He made it noble above being sorcery, soothsaying, or lies. It was also said that it is noble because of the noble characteristics and lofty matters it contains. It was also said that it is because it honours its memorizer and magnifies its reciter.

Al-Wāḥidī related from the people of meanings (*ahl al-maʿānī*) that the description of the Qur'an as *karīm* (noble) is because it is in its nature to give abundant good through the proofs that lead to the truth in religion. Al-Azharī said: *al-karīm* is a comprehensive term for what is praiseworthy, and the Qur'an is noble, praised for the guidance, clarification, knowledge and wisdom it contains.

﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾, meaning hidden and protected. It was said: safeguarded from falsehood, and this is the *al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ* (the Preserved Tablet), as a group said. It was also said that it is a book. ʿIkrimah said: it is the Torah and the Gospel, in which the Qur'an and the one to whom it is revealed are mentioned. Al-Suddī said: it is the Psalms (*al-Zabūr*). Mujāhid and Qatādah said: it is the codex (*muṣḥaf*) that is in our hands.

﴿None touches it but the purified﴾. Al-Wāḥidī said: most exegetes hold that the pronoun refers to the Book that is well-guarded, meaning: none touches the Book that is well-guarded except the purified, and they are the angels. It was said they are the angels and the messengers from among the children of Adam. The meaning of "does not touch it" is actual touching. It was also said its meaning is: none descends with it except the purified. It was said its meaning is: none recites it. On the view that the intended Book is the Qur'an, it was said that ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾ means: purified from ritual impurities (*aḥdāth*) and filth (*anjās*). So said Qatādah and others. al-Kalbī said: "the purified" are those purified from *shirk* (polytheism). al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: those purified from sins and faults. Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl and others said: the meaning of ﴿does not touch it﴾ is: none recites it except the purified, that is, except the monotheists (*al-muwaḥḥidūn*). al-Farrāʾ said: none obtains its benefit and blessing except the purified, that is, the believers. al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl said: none knows its interpretation and explanation except one whom Allah has purified from *shirk* and hypocrisy.

The majority held that one in a state of ritual impurity (*muḥdith*) is forbidden from touching the codex (*muṣḥaf*). This was said by ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Saʿīd ibn Zayd, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Zuhrī, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥakam, Ḥammād, and a group of jurists, among them Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Shaʿbī, and a group including Abū Ḥanīfah that it is permissible for the one in a state of ritual impurity to touch it. We have clarified what is the truth in this matter in our commentary on *al-Muntaqā*, so let one refer to it.

The majority recited ﴿al-muṭahharūn﴾ with a light *ṭāʾ* and a heavy *hāʾ* with a fatḥah, as a passive participle (*ism mafʿūl*). Salmān al-Fārisī recited it with a kasrah on the *hāʾ*, as an active participle (*ism fāʿil*), meaning: those who purify themselves. Nāfiʿ, and Ibn ʿUmar in one narration from him, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, recited it with a sukūn on the *ṭāʾ* and a fatḥah on the *hāʾ*, lightly, as a passive participle from *aṭhara*. al-Ḥasan, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf recited it with a heavy *ṭāʾ* and a kasrah on the *hāʾ*, and its original form is *al-mutaṭahharūn*.

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. The majority recited it in the nominative (*rafʿ*), and it was also recited in the accusative (*naṣb*). The nominative is because it is another adjective of *qurʾān*, or the predicate of an omitted subject, while the accusative is as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*).

﴿Then is it this discourse that you are scornful of?﴾ The demonstrative refers to the Qur'an, described by the preceding attributes. The *mudhin* and *mudāhin* are the hypocrite. So said al-Zajjāj and others. ʿAṭāʾ and others said: it is the liar. Muqātil ibn Sulaymān and Qatādah said: *mudhinūn* means disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9]. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: *mudhinūn* means those who turn away. Mujāhid said: those who side with the disbelievers in disbelief. Abū Kaysān said: *al-mudhin* is one who does not recognise the right of Allah upon him and wards it off with excuses.

The first view is preferable, because the origin of *mudhin* is one whose outward appearance differs from his inward reality, as if he resembles oil (*duhn*) in its smoothness. al-Muʾarrij said: *al-mudhin* is the hypocrite who softens in order to conceal his disbelief. *Al-idhān* and *al-mudāhanah* are denial, disbelief and hypocrisy. Its origin is softness, and to conceal the opposite of what one displays. In *al-Kashshāf* it is said: *mudhinūn*, meaning: those who are lax regarding it, like one who "*yudhin*" in a matter, that is, who softens his side and does not stand firm in it out of laxity regarding it. End of quote.

al-Rāghib said: *al-idhān* originally is like *al-tadhīn* (anointing with oil), but it has become an expression for flattery (*al-mudārāh*) and softness (*al-mulāyanah*), and abandoning seriousness, just as *al-taqrīd* (removing ticks) became an expression for that. What he mentioned is supported by the saying of Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat:

"Resolve and strength are better than flattery, and the timid and the cowardly."

﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ There is an omitted genitive (*muḍāf maḥdhūf*) in the speech, as al-Wāḥidī related from the exegetes, meaning: you make the thanks for your provision that you deny the blessing of Allah, so you place denial in the place of thanks. Al-Haytham said: the Azd Shanūʾah say *mā ruziqa fulānun*, meaning: "he did not give thanks." According to this dialect, there is no omitted genitive in the verse, rather the meaning of *rizq* (provision) is thanks. The reason for expressing thanks by *rizq* is that thanks overflows with an increase of provision, so thanks becomes a provision, expressing the cause by the effect (*taʿbīr bil-sabab ʿan al-musabbab*). Among what falls under this verse is the saying of the disbelievers when Allah gives them drink and sends rain down upon them: "We were given drink by such-and-such a star, and we were given rain by such-and-such a star."

al-Azharī said: the meaning of the verse is: instead of thanking Him, you make your provision, which Allah has provided you, the denial that it is from Allah the Provider.

ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās recited *wa-tajʿalūna shukrakum* ("and you make your thanks"). The majority recited ﴿annakum tukadhdhibūn﴾ with a doubled *dhāl* from *al-takdhīb* (denial), while ʿAlī and ʿĀṣim, in one narration from him, recited it with a light *dhāl* from *al-kadhib* (lying).

﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat﴾, meaning: then why not, when the soul or the self reaches the throat at death. No reference to it has preceded, because the meaning is understood by them when they use such an expression. From this is the saying of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī:

"O Māwiyyah, wealth does not avail a man when the death-rattle takes him one day and the chest constricts upon it."

﴿And you at that moment are looking on﴾, at what he is in, that one whose soul or spirit has reached the throat.

al-Zajjāj said: "And you, O people of the dead, in that state, see the dead one as he has come to the point of his soul leaving. The meaning is that in that state they cannot repel it from him, and they cannot do anything that benefits him or lightens what he is in."

﴿And We are nearer to him than you﴾, meaning by knowledge, power and sight. It was said: He meant that Our messengers, who take charge of seizing him, are nearer to him than you. ﴿But you do not perceive﴾, meaning you do not comprehend that, due to your ignorance that Allah is nearer to His servant than his jugular vein. Or: you do not see the angels of death who attend the dead one and take charge of seizing him.

﴿Then why, if you are not to be judged﴾ ﴿you do not return it?﴾ It is said: *dāna al-sulṭānu raʿiyyatahu*, when the ruler governed his subjects and enslaved them. Al-Farrāʾ said: *dintuhu*: I possessed him. He recited for al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"You have indeed governed the affairs of your sons, until you left them finer than flour."

That is, you possessed them. It is also said *dānahu* means he humbled him and enslaved him. It was said the meaning of *madīnīna* is those called to account (*muḥāsabūn*), and it was said: those who will be recompensed (*majziyyūn*), and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Nothing remains but the enemies; we have repaid them as they repaid."

The first meaning is closer to the sense of the verse, that is: then why, if you are not those who are ruled and owned, do you not return it, namely the soul which has reached the throat, to its place where it was? ﴿If you are truthful﴾, and you will not return it, so your claim that you are not ruled nor owned is refuted. The operator of *idhā balaghat* ("when it reaches") is *turjiʿūnahā* ("you return it"), and the second *lawlā* is an emphasis for the first. al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs sometimes repeat the two particles while their meaning is one.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the classes of creation at death and after it, saying: ﴿As for if he is of those brought near﴾, meaning the foremost among the three categories whose details have preceded. ﴿Then rest and provision and a Garden of bliss﴾. Most recited *rawḥun* with a fatḥah on the *rāʾ*, and its meaning is rest from worldly life and relief from their conditions. al-Ḥasan said: *al-rawḥ* is mercy. Mujāhid said: *al-rawḥ* is joy. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, and al-Jaḥdarī recited *fa-rūḥun* with a ḍammah on the *rāʾ*, and this recitation is related from Yaʿqūb, and it is said also from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Muqātil. Muqātil said: it is *al-rizq* (provision) in the dialect of Ḥimyar; one says: "I went out seeking *rayḥān Allāh*," meaning His provision. From this is the saying of al-Namir ibn Tawlab:

"The peace of God and His *rayḥān*, and His mercy, and abundant rain."

Qatādah said: it is the Garden. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is mercy. al-Ḥasan said: it is the well-known *rayḥān* that is smelled. Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: this is at death, and the Garden is kept hidden for him until he is resurrected. Abū al-Jawzāʾ and Abū al-ʿĀliyah said likewise. The meaning of "and a Garden of bliss" is that it is full of luxury. The *rawḥ* and what follows it are in the nominative as the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and the predicate is omitted, meaning: then for him is rest.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 56, verses 75–96 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And as for if he was﴾ that deceased person ﴿one of the companions of the right﴾, and their conditions and the reward Allah has prepared for them have already been mentioned and detailed, ﴿then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾. That is: you will not see among them except what you love of safety, so do not be concerned for them, for they will be safe from the punishment of Allah. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Peace be upon you from them," that is, you are free from distress over them. It has been said that the meaning is: they pray for you and greet you with peace. It has been said that he (ﷺ) is greeted with peace out of honour. It has been said that it is a report from Allah, glorified is He, that some of them greet others with peace. It has been said that the meaning is: "Peace be upon you, O companion of the right, from your brethren, the companions of the right."

﴿And as for if he was one of the deniers, the astray﴾, that is, the deniers of the Resurrection, those who went astray from guidance, and they are the companions of the left, whose mention has preceded and whose conditions have been detailed, ﴿then there is a welcome of boiling water﴾, that is: for him there is a welcome prepared for his arrival, of boiling water (*hamim*), which is water whose heat has reached its extreme. This is after he has eaten from the *zaqqum* as its explanation has preceded.

﴿And the burning of the Hellfire﴾. It is said *aslahu al-nar* and *sallahu*, meaning: when he is placed into the Fire. This is an *idafa* (genitive construction) of the verbal noun to the object, or to the place.

Al-Mubarrad said: The response (*jawab*) of the conditional particle in these three places is omitted, and the estimate is: "Whatever may be the case, then there is rest, etc."

Al-Akhfash said: the *fa'* (the particle *fa*) in the three places is the response of *amma* and the response of the conditional particle together.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿wa-tasliyatu﴾ in the nominative, coordinated upon "fanuzulun" (*fa-nuzulun*). Abu 'Amr, in one of the transmissions from him, read it in the genitive, coordinated upon "hamim" (*min hamim*): that is, "then a welcome of boiling water and of the burning of the Hellfire."

﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty﴾. The reference is to what has been mentioned in this surah, or to what was mentioned shortly before of the conditions of the three groups. It is the true certainty, that is: its pure and unmixed essence. The *idafa* of *haqq* (truth) to *yaqin* (certainty) is of the type of attributing a thing to itself.

Al-Mubarrad said: it is like your saying "*'ayn al-yaqin*" (the eye of certainty) and "*mahd al-yaqin*" (the pure certainty). This is according to the Kufans, and they permitted it because of the difference of wording. As for the Basrans, they hold that the second term of the *idafa* is omitted, and the estimate is: "the true matter of certainty" or "the true report of certainty."

The *fa'* in ﴿so glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it: that is, declare Him free of what does not befit His majesty. The *ba'* (the preposition *bi*) is connected to an omitted element: that is, "so glorify, being associated with the name of your Lord," for blessing through it.

It has been said that the meaning is: "so pray, mentioning your Lord." It has been said that the *ba'* is superfluous, and *al-ism* (the name) means the essence.

It has been said that it indicates transitivity, because *sabbih* (glorify) is transitive by itself at times and transitive by a preposition at other times, and the first is preferable.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* (*Shu'ab al-Iman*) transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Qur'an was sent down in the Night of Decree (*Laylat al-Qadr*) from the highest heaven to the lowest heaven all at once, and then it was revealed in portions over the years." In another wording: "Then it descended from the lowest heaven to the earth in stars (*nujum*)." Then he recited: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him regarding ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ that he said: "The Qur'an." ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾, he said: "The Qur'an."

Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him regarding the verse: "The stars of the Qur'an, when it descends."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ma'rifa* transmitted from several chains from Ibn 'Abbas also regarding ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾ that he said: "The Book that is sent down in the heaven, none touches it but the angels."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Anas regarding ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾ that he said: "The angels."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Alqama, who said: "We came to Salman al-Farisi, and he came out to us from a *kanif* (latrine). We said to him: 'If only you had performed ablution, O Abu 'Abd Allah, and then recited to us such-and-such a surah.' He said: 'Allah only said ﴿in a Book well-protected﴾ ﴿none touches it but the purified﴾, and it is the one that is in the heaven, none touches it but the angels.' Then he recited to us from the Qur'an whatever we wished."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Dawud, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, from his father, who said: "In the letter of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'Amr ibn Hazm: 'None should touch the Qur'an except in a state of purity.'"

Malik transmitted it in *al-Muwatta'* from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr.

Abu Dawud transmitted it in *al-Marasil* (the collection of *mursal* reports) from the hadith of al-Zuhri, who said: "He read in the manuscript of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'None who is not pure should touch the Qur'an.'" Al-Daraqutni traced it back to 'Amr ibn Hazm, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, and 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, but there is scrutiny regarding their chains.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Umar that he would not touch the *mushaf* (the codex) except when in a state of ablution.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba in *al-Musannaf*, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, who said: "We were with Salman, and he set off for a need, then he hid from us, then came out to us. We said: 'If only you had performed ablution, so we could ask you about some matters of the Qur'an.' He said: 'Ask me, for I will not touch it; only the purified touch it.' Then he recited ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None who is not pure should touch the Qur'an." Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that when the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to Yemen, he wrote for him in his instructions: "That none who is not pure should touch the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Do you then disbelieve/ are you [of those who] deny?﴾ (*mudhinun*) that he said: "Deniers (*mukadhdhibun*)."

Muslim, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The people were given rain during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'In the morning some of the people are thankful and some of them are disbelievers. They said: "This is a mercy that Allah has placed." And some of them said: "Such-and-such a *nawʾ* (star-rising) has indeed brought it." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ until ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾'" The essence of the hadith, without mention that it is the cause of the revelation of the verse, is established in the two *Sahihs* from the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani and from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

There are other hadiths on this subject.

Ahmad, Ibn Mani', 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it *hasan*), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtara* transmitted from 'Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾ that he said: "Your thanks (*shukrakum*). You say: 'We were given rain by such-and-such a *nawʾ* and by such-and-such a star.'"

Ibn 'Asakir in his *Tarikh* transmitted from 'A'isha who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not explain from the Qur'an except a few easy verses."

Regarding His saying ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾, he said: "Your thanks."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Ali that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited '*wa-taj'alna shukrakum*' (and you make your thanks)."

Abu 'Ubayd in *Fada'il al-Qur'an*, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to read "*wa-taj'alna shukrakum*" and said: "He means the star-risings (*al-anwa'*). No people were given rain except that some of them became disbelievers. They used to say: 'We were given rain by such-and-such a star-rising.' So Allah revealed ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from 'Ali, that he read "*wa-taj'alna shukrakum*" and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reading it in this way."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿not subject to judgement (*ghayra madinin*)﴾ that he said: "Not held to account."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* (*Kitab al-Zuhd*), 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym regarding ﴿And as for if he was one of those brought near﴾ — the verse — that he said: "This is for him at death. ﴿And a garden of delight﴾: the Garden is kept hidden for him until the Day he is resurrected. ﴿And as for if he was one of the deniers, the astray﴾ ﴿then there is a welcome of boiling water﴾," he said: "This is at death. ﴿And the burning of the Hellfire﴾," he said: "The Hellfire is kept hidden for him until the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿then rest﴾ that he said: "Fragrance (*ra'iha*)." ﴿And sweet basil (*rayhan*)﴾, he said: "Relief (*istirahah*)."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: "By *al-rayhan* is meant one who is relieved from this world." ﴿And a garden of delight﴾ — he says: "Forgiveness and mercy."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also that he said: "*Al-rayhan* is provision (*al-rizq*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also regarding His saying ﴿Then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾ that he said: "The angels come to him with peace from Allah; they greet him and inform him that he is of the companions of the right."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: ﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty﴾, he said: "What We have related to you in this surah."

He transmitted from him also: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, he said: "Pray to your Lord."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir al-Juhani, who said: "When ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: 'Make it in your *ruku'* (bowing).' Then when ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed, he said: 'Make it in your *sujud* (prostration).'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 56, verses 75–96 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿So I swear not﴾. The majority of the exegetes held that "lā" (لا) is superfluous, for emphasis, and the meaning is "so I swear." This is supported by His later saying, ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you knew﴾. A group of exegetes said that it is for negation, and that what is negated by it is omitted, namely the speech of the disbelieving deniers. Al-Farrā' said: "It is a negation, and the meaning is: the matter is not as you say. Then he began anew and said: 'I swear.'" This was deemed weak, because omitting the subject and predicate of "lā" is not permissible, as Abū Ḥayyān and others said.

It was also said that it is the *lām al-ibtidā'* (the emphatic lām), and the original is *fa-la-uqsimu*, with the fatḥah lengthened so that an alif was produced from it, as in the words of the poet: "I seek refuge in God from the scorpion." Al-Ḥasan, Ḥumayd and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited it thus, *fa-la-uqsimu*, without an alif. According to this view and this recitation (*qirāʾah*), an omitted subject is assumed, and the estimate is: "So as for me, I swear by that."

It was also said that "lā" here has the meaning of "*alā*," the one used for alerting, but this is far-fetched.

It was said that "lā" here is in its literal sense, and that it negates the oath, meaning: "So I do not swear upon this, because the matter is clearer than that." This is rejected by His saying, ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you knew﴾, together with the specification of what is sworn by and what is sworn to.

The meaning of His saying ﴿the setting-places of the stars﴾ is their *masāqiṭ* (places of setting), which are their western points, as Qatādah and others said. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: their *manāzil* (mansions). Al-Ḥasan said: their dispersal and scattering on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they are the *anwāʾ* (star-risings) that the people of the Jāhiliyyah used to say, "We were given rain by the *nawʾ* of such-and-such."

It was also said that the intended meaning of "the setting-places of the stars" is the descent of the Qur'an in parts (*nujūman*) from the *al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ* (the Preserved Tablet). Al-Suddī and others said this. Al-Farrā' related from Ibn Masʿūd that the setting-places of the stars are the *muḥkam* (clear, decisive verses) of the Qur'an.

The majority recited *mawāqiʿi* in the plural, while Ibn Masʿūd, al-Nakhaʿī, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Warsh from Yaʿqūb recited *bi-mawqiʿi* in the singular. Al-Mubarrad said: "*Mawqiʿ* here is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), so it may be singular or plural."

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of the magnification and exaltation of this oath, saying: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you knew﴾. This sentence is a parenthetical clause (*muʿtaraḍah*) between the thing sworn by and the thing sworn to. His saying ﴿if you knew﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the two parts of the parenthetical clause, so it is a parenthesis within a parenthesis.

Al-Farrā' and al-Zajjāj said: "This indicates that the intended meaning of the setting-places of the stars is the descent of the Qur'an. The pronoun in *innahu* refers to the oath implied by *uqsimu* (I swear). The meaning is: indeed the oath by the setting-places of the stars is a mighty oath, if you knew."

Then He mentioned the thing sworn to, saying: ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, meaning: Allah honoured it, made it mighty, and raised its status above all the Books. He made it noble above being sorcery, soothsaying, or lies. It was also said that it is noble because of the noble characteristics and lofty matters it contains. It was also said that it is because it honours its memorizer and magnifies its reciter.

Al-Wāḥidī related from the people of meanings (*ahl al-maʿānī*) that the description of the Qur'an as *karīm* (noble) is because it is in its nature to give abundant good through the proofs that lead to the truth in religion. Al-Azharī said: *al-karīm* is a comprehensive term for what is praiseworthy, and the Qur'an is noble, praised for the guidance, clarification, knowledge and wisdom it contains.

﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾, meaning hidden and protected. It was said: safeguarded from falsehood, and this is the *al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ* (the Preserved Tablet), as a group said. It was also said that it is a book. ʿIkrimah said: it is the Torah and the Gospel, in which the Qur'an and the one to whom it is revealed are mentioned. Al-Suddī said: it is the Psalms (*al-Zabūr*). Mujāhid and Qatādah said: it is the codex (*muṣḥaf*) that is in our hands.

﴿None touches it but the purified﴾. Al-Wāḥidī said: most exegetes hold that the pronoun refers to the Book that is well-guarded, meaning: none touches the Book that is well-guarded except the purified, and they are the angels. It was said they are the angels and the messengers from among the children of Adam. The meaning of "does not touch it" is actual touching. It was also said its meaning is: none descends with it except the purified. It was said its meaning is: none recites it. On the view that the intended Book is the Qur'an, it was said that ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾ means: purified from ritual impurities (*aḥdāth*) and filth (*anjās*). So said Qatādah and others. al-Kalbī said: "the purified" are those purified from *shirk* (polytheism). al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: those purified from sins and faults. Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl and others said: the meaning of ﴿does not touch it﴾ is: none recites it except the purified, that is, except the monotheists (*al-muwaḥḥidūn*). al-Farrāʾ said: none obtains its benefit and blessing except the purified, that is, the believers. al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl said: none knows its interpretation and explanation except one whom Allah has purified from *shirk* and hypocrisy.

The majority held that one in a state of ritual impurity (*muḥdith*) is forbidden from touching the codex (*muṣḥaf*). This was said by ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Saʿīd ibn Zayd, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Zuhrī, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥakam, Ḥammād, and a group of jurists, among them Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Shaʿbī, and a group including Abū Ḥanīfah that it is permissible for the one in a state of ritual impurity to touch it. We have clarified what is the truth in this matter in our commentary on *al-Muntaqā*, so let one refer to it.

The majority recited ﴿al-muṭahharūn﴾ with a light *ṭāʾ* and a heavy *hāʾ* with a fatḥah, as a passive participle (*ism mafʿūl*). Salmān al-Fārisī recited it with a kasrah on the *hāʾ*, as an active participle (*ism fāʿil*), meaning: those who purify themselves. Nāfiʿ, and Ibn ʿUmar in one narration from him, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, recited it with a sukūn on the *ṭāʾ* and a fatḥah on the *hāʾ*, lightly, as a passive participle from *aṭhara*. al-Ḥasan, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf recited it with a heavy *ṭāʾ* and a kasrah on the *hāʾ*, and its original form is *al-mutaṭahharūn*.

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. The majority recited it in the nominative (*rafʿ*), and it was also recited in the accusative (*naṣb*). The nominative is because it is another adjective of *qurʾān*, or the predicate of an omitted subject, while the accusative is as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*).

﴿Then is it this discourse that you are scornful of?﴾ The demonstrative refers to the Qur'an, described by the preceding attributes. The *mudhin* and *mudāhin* are the hypocrite. So said al-Zajjāj and others. ʿAṭāʾ and others said: it is the liar. Muqātil ibn Sulaymān and Qatādah said: *mudhinūn* means disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9]. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: *mudhinūn* means those who turn away. Mujāhid said: those who side with the disbelievers in disbelief. Abū Kaysān said: *al-mudhin* is one who does not recognise the right of Allah upon him and wards it off with excuses.

The first view is preferable, because the origin of *mudhin* is one whose outward appearance differs from his inward reality, as if he resembles oil (*duhn*) in its smoothness. al-Muʾarrij said: *al-mudhin* is the hypocrite who softens in order to conceal his disbelief. *Al-idhān* and *al-mudāhanah* are denial, disbelief and hypocrisy. Its origin is softness, and to conceal the opposite of what one displays. In *al-Kashshāf* it is said: *mudhinūn*, meaning: those who are lax regarding it, like one who "*yudhin*" in a matter, that is, who softens his side and does not stand firm in it out of laxity regarding it. End of quote.

al-Rāghib said: *al-idhān* originally is like *al-tadhīn* (anointing with oil), but it has become an expression for flattery (*al-mudārāh*) and softness (*al-mulāyanah*), and abandoning seriousness, just as *al-taqrīd* (removing ticks) became an expression for that. What he mentioned is supported by the saying of Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat:

"Resolve and strength are better than flattery, and the timid and the cowardly."

﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ There is an omitted genitive (*muḍāf maḥdhūf*) in the speech, as al-Wāḥidī related from the exegetes, meaning: you make the thanks for your provision that you deny the blessing of Allah, so you place denial in the place of thanks. Al-Haytham said: the Azd Shanūʾah say *mā ruziqa fulānun*, meaning: "he did not give thanks." According to this dialect, there is no omitted genitive in the verse, rather the meaning of *rizq* (provision) is thanks. The reason for expressing thanks by *rizq* is that thanks overflows with an increase of provision, so thanks becomes a provision, expressing the cause by the effect (*taʿbīr bil-sabab ʿan al-musabbab*). Among what falls under this verse is the saying of the disbelievers when Allah gives them drink and sends rain down upon them: "We were given drink by such-and-such a star, and we were given rain by such-and-such a star."

al-Azharī said: the meaning of the verse is: instead of thanking Him, you make your provision, which Allah has provided you, the denial that it is from Allah the Provider.

ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās recited *wa-tajʿalūna shukrakum* ("and you make your thanks"). The majority recited ﴿annakum tukadhdhibūn﴾ with a doubled *dhāl* from *al-takdhīb* (denial), while ʿAlī and ʿĀṣim, in one narration from him, recited it with a light *dhāl* from *al-kadhib* (lying).

﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat﴾, meaning: then why not, when the soul or the self reaches the throat at death. No reference to it has preceded, because the meaning is understood by them when they use such an expression. From this is the saying of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī:

"O Māwiyyah, wealth does not avail a man when the death-rattle takes him one day and the chest constricts upon it."

﴿And you at that moment are looking on﴾, at what he is in, that one whose soul or spirit has reached the throat.

al-Zajjāj said: "And you, O people of the dead, in that state, see the dead one as he has come to the point of his soul leaving. The meaning is that in that state they cannot repel it from him, and they cannot do anything that benefits him or lightens what he is in."

﴿And We are nearer to him than you﴾, meaning by knowledge, power and sight. It was said: He meant that Our messengers, who take charge of seizing him, are nearer to him than you. ﴿But you do not perceive﴾, meaning you do not comprehend that, due to your ignorance that Allah is nearer to His servant than his jugular vein. Or: you do not see the angels of death who attend the dead one and take charge of seizing him.

﴿Then why, if you are not to be judged﴾ ﴿you do not return it?﴾ It is said: *dāna al-sulṭānu raʿiyyatahu*, when the ruler governed his subjects and enslaved them. Al-Farrāʾ said: *dintuhu*: I possessed him. He recited for al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"You have indeed governed the affairs of your sons, until you left them finer than flour."

That is, you possessed them. It is also said *dānahu* means he humbled him and enslaved him. It was said the meaning of *madīnīna* is those called to account (*muḥāsabūn*), and it was said: those who will be recompensed (*majziyyūn*), and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Nothing remains but the enemies; we have repaid them as they repaid."

The first meaning is closer to the sense of the verse, that is: then why, if you are not those who are ruled and owned, do you not return it, namely the soul which has reached the throat, to its place where it was? ﴿If you are truthful﴾, and you will not return it, so your claim that you are not ruled nor owned is refuted. The operator of *idhā balaghat* ("when it reaches") is *turjiʿūnahā* ("you return it"), and the second *lawlā* is an emphasis for the first. al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs sometimes repeat the two particles while their meaning is one.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the classes of creation at death and after it, saying: ﴿As for if he is of those brought near﴾, meaning the foremost among the three categories whose details have preceded. ﴿Then rest and provision and a Garden of bliss﴾. Most recited *rawḥun* with a fatḥah on the *rāʾ*, and its meaning is rest from worldly life and relief from their conditions. al-Ḥasan said: *al-rawḥ* is mercy. Mujāhid said: *al-rawḥ* is joy. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, and al-Jaḥdarī recited *fa-rūḥun* with a ḍammah on the *rāʾ*, and this recitation is related from Yaʿqūb, and it is said also from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Muqātil. Muqātil said: it is *al-rizq* (provision) in the dialect of Ḥimyar; one says: "I went out seeking *rayḥān Allāh*," meaning His provision. From this is the saying of al-Namir ibn Tawlab:

"The peace of God and His *rayḥān*, and His mercy, and abundant rain."

Qatādah said: it is the Garden. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is mercy. al-Ḥasan said: it is the well-known *rayḥān* that is smelled. Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: this is at death, and the Garden is kept hidden for him until he is resurrected. Abū al-Jawzāʾ and Abū al-ʿĀliyah said likewise. The meaning of "and a Garden of bliss" is that it is full of luxury. The *rawḥ* and what follows it are in the nominative as the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and the predicate is omitted, meaning: then for him is rest.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 56, verses 75–96 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And as for if he was﴾ that deceased person ﴿one of the companions of the right﴾, and their conditions and the reward Allah has prepared for them have already been mentioned and detailed, ﴿then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾. That is: you will not see among them except what you love of safety, so do not be concerned for them, for they will be safe from the punishment of Allah. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Peace be upon you from them," that is, you are free from distress over them. It has been said that the meaning is: they pray for you and greet you with peace. It has been said that he (ﷺ) is greeted with peace out of honour. It has been said that it is a report from Allah, glorified is He, that some of them greet others with peace. It has been said that the meaning is: "Peace be upon you, O companion of the right, from your brethren, the companions of the right."

﴿And as for if he was one of the deniers, the astray﴾, that is, the deniers of the Resurrection, those who went astray from guidance, and they are the companions of the left, whose mention has preceded and whose conditions have been detailed, ﴿then there is a welcome of boiling water﴾, that is: for him there is a welcome prepared for his arrival, of boiling water (*hamim*), which is water whose heat has reached its extreme. This is after he has eaten from the *zaqqum* as its explanation has preceded.

﴿And the burning of the Hellfire﴾. It is said *aslahu al-nar* and *sallahu*, meaning: when he is placed into the Fire. This is an *idafa* (genitive construction) of the verbal noun to the object, or to the place.

Al-Mubarrad said: The response (*jawab*) of the conditional particle in these three places is omitted, and the estimate is: "Whatever may be the case, then there is rest, etc."

Al-Akhfash said: the *fa'* (the particle *fa*) in the three places is the response of *amma* and the response of the conditional particle together.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿wa-tasliyatu﴾ in the nominative, coordinated upon "fanuzulun" (*fa-nuzulun*). Abu 'Amr, in one of the transmissions from him, read it in the genitive, coordinated upon "hamim" (*min hamim*): that is, "then a welcome of boiling water and of the burning of the Hellfire."

﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty﴾. The reference is to what has been mentioned in this surah, or to what was mentioned shortly before of the conditions of the three groups. It is the true certainty, that is: its pure and unmixed essence. The *idafa* of *haqq* (truth) to *yaqin* (certainty) is of the type of attributing a thing to itself.

Al-Mubarrad said: it is like your saying "*'ayn al-yaqin*" (the eye of certainty) and "*mahd al-yaqin*" (the pure certainty). This is according to the Kufans, and they permitted it because of the difference of wording. As for the Basrans, they hold that the second term of the *idafa* is omitted, and the estimate is: "the true matter of certainty" or "the true report of certainty."

The *fa'* in ﴿so glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it: that is, declare Him free of what does not befit His majesty. The *ba'* (the preposition *bi*) is connected to an omitted element: that is, "so glorify, being associated with the name of your Lord," for blessing through it.

It has been said that the meaning is: "so pray, mentioning your Lord." It has been said that the *ba'* is superfluous, and *al-ism* (the name) means the essence.

It has been said that it indicates transitivity, because *sabbih* (glorify) is transitive by itself at times and transitive by a preposition at other times, and the first is preferable.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* (*Shu'ab al-Iman*) transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Qur'an was sent down in the Night of Decree (*Laylat al-Qadr*) from the highest heaven to the lowest heaven all at once, and then it was revealed in portions over the years." In another wording: "Then it descended from the lowest heaven to the earth in stars (*nujum*)." Then he recited: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him regarding ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ that he said: "The Qur'an." ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾, he said: "The Qur'an."

Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him regarding the verse: "The stars of the Qur'an, when it descends."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ma'rifa* transmitted from several chains from Ibn 'Abbas also regarding ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾ that he said: "The Book that is sent down in the heaven, none touches it but the angels."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Anas regarding ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾ that he said: "The angels."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Alqama, who said: "We came to Salman al-Farisi, and he came out to us from a *kanif* (latrine). We said to him: 'If only you had performed ablution, O Abu 'Abd Allah, and then recited to us such-and-such a surah.' He said: 'Allah only said ﴿in a Book well-protected﴾ ﴿none touches it but the purified﴾, and it is the one that is in the heaven, none touches it but the angels.' Then he recited to us from the Qur'an whatever we wished."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Dawud, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, from his father, who said: "In the letter of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'Amr ibn Hazm: 'None should touch the Qur'an except in a state of purity.'"

Malik transmitted it in *al-Muwatta'* from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr.

Abu Dawud transmitted it in *al-Marasil* (the collection of *mursal* reports) from the hadith of al-Zuhri, who said: "He read in the manuscript of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'None who is not pure should touch the Qur'an.'" Al-Daraqutni traced it back to 'Amr ibn Hazm, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, and 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, but there is scrutiny regarding their chains.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Umar that he would not touch the *mushaf* (the codex) except when in a state of ablution.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba in *al-Musannaf*, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, who said: "We were with Salman, and he set off for a need, then he hid from us, then came out to us. We said: 'If only you had performed ablution, so we could ask you about some matters of the Qur'an.' He said: 'Ask me, for I will not touch it; only the purified touch it.' Then he recited ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None who is not pure should touch the Qur'an." Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that when the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to Yemen, he wrote for him in his instructions: "That none who is not pure should touch the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Do you then disbelieve/ are you [of those who] deny?﴾ (*mudhinun*) that he said: "Deniers (*mukadhdhibun*)."

Muslim, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The people were given rain during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'In the morning some of the people are thankful and some of them are disbelievers. They said: "This is a mercy that Allah has placed." And some of them said: "Such-and-such a *nawʾ* (star-rising) has indeed brought it." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ until ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾'" The essence of the hadith, without mention that it is the cause of the revelation of the verse, is established in the two *Sahihs* from the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani and from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

There are other hadiths on this subject.

Ahmad, Ibn Mani', 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it *hasan*), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtara* transmitted from 'Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾ that he said: "Your thanks (*shukrakum*). You say: 'We were given rain by such-and-such a *nawʾ* and by such-and-such a star.'"

Ibn 'Asakir in his *Tarikh* transmitted from 'A'isha who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not explain from the Qur'an except a few easy verses."

Regarding His saying ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾, he said: "Your thanks."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Ali that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited '*wa-taj'alna shukrakum*' (and you make your thanks)."

Abu 'Ubayd in *Fada'il al-Qur'an*, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to read "*wa-taj'alna shukrakum*" and said: "He means the star-risings (*al-anwa'*). No people were given rain except that some of them became disbelievers. They used to say: 'We were given rain by such-and-such a star-rising.' So Allah revealed ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from 'Ali, that he read "*wa-taj'alna shukrakum*" and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reading it in this way."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿not subject to judgement (*ghayra madinin*)﴾ that he said: "Not held to account."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* (*Kitab al-Zuhd*), 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym regarding ﴿And as for if he was one of those brought near﴾ — the verse — that he said: "This is for him at death. ﴿And a garden of delight﴾: the Garden is kept hidden for him until the Day he is resurrected. ﴿And as for if he was one of the deniers, the astray﴾ ﴿then there is a welcome of boiling water﴾," he said: "This is at death. ﴿And the burning of the Hellfire﴾," he said: "The Hellfire is kept hidden for him until the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿then rest﴾ that he said: "Fragrance (*ra'iha*)." ﴿And sweet basil (*rayhan*)﴾, he said: "Relief (*istirahah*)."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: "By *al-rayhan* is meant one who is relieved from this world." ﴿And a garden of delight﴾ — he says: "Forgiveness and mercy."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also that he said: "*Al-rayhan* is provision (*al-rizq*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also regarding His saying ﴿Then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾ that he said: "The angels come to him with peace from Allah; they greet him and inform him that he is of the companions of the right."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: ﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty﴾, he said: "What We have related to you in this surah."

He transmitted from him also: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, he said: "Pray to your Lord."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir al-Juhani, who said: "When ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: 'Make it in your *ruku'* (bowing).' Then when ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed, he said: 'Make it in your *sujud* (prostration).'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 56, verses 75–96 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿So I swear not﴾. The majority of the exegetes held that "lā" (لا) is superfluous, for emphasis, and the meaning is "so I swear." This is supported by His later saying, ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you knew﴾. A group of exegetes said that it is for negation, and that what is negated by it is omitted, namely the speech of the disbelieving deniers. Al-Farrā' said: "It is a negation, and the meaning is: the matter is not as you say. Then he began anew and said: 'I swear.'" This was deemed weak, because omitting the subject and predicate of "lā" is not permissible, as Abū Ḥayyān and others said.

It was also said that it is the *lām al-ibtidā'* (the emphatic lām), and the original is *fa-la-uqsimu*, with the fatḥah lengthened so that an alif was produced from it, as in the words of the poet: "I seek refuge in God from the scorpion." Al-Ḥasan, Ḥumayd and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited it thus, *fa-la-uqsimu*, without an alif. According to this view and this recitation (*qirāʾah*), an omitted subject is assumed, and the estimate is: "So as for me, I swear by that."

It was also said that "lā" here has the meaning of "*alā*," the one used for alerting, but this is far-fetched.

It was said that "lā" here is in its literal sense, and that it negates the oath, meaning: "So I do not swear upon this, because the matter is clearer than that." This is rejected by His saying, ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you knew﴾, together with the specification of what is sworn by and what is sworn to.

The meaning of His saying ﴿the setting-places of the stars﴾ is their *masāqiṭ* (places of setting), which are their western points, as Qatādah and others said. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: their *manāzil* (mansions). Al-Ḥasan said: their dispersal and scattering on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they are the *anwāʾ* (star-risings) that the people of the Jāhiliyyah used to say, "We were given rain by the *nawʾ* of such-and-such."

It was also said that the intended meaning of "the setting-places of the stars" is the descent of the Qur'an in parts (*nujūman*) from the *al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ* (the Preserved Tablet). Al-Suddī and others said this. Al-Farrā' related from Ibn Masʿūd that the setting-places of the stars are the *muḥkam* (clear, decisive verses) of the Qur'an.

The majority recited *mawāqiʿi* in the plural, while Ibn Masʿūd, al-Nakhaʿī, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Warsh from Yaʿqūb recited *bi-mawqiʿi* in the singular. Al-Mubarrad said: "*Mawqiʿ* here is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), so it may be singular or plural."

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of the magnification and exaltation of this oath, saying: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you knew﴾. This sentence is a parenthetical clause (*muʿtaraḍah*) between the thing sworn by and the thing sworn to. His saying ﴿if you knew﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the two parts of the parenthetical clause, so it is a parenthesis within a parenthesis.

Al-Farrā' and al-Zajjāj said: "This indicates that the intended meaning of the setting-places of the stars is the descent of the Qur'an. The pronoun in *innahu* refers to the oath implied by *uqsimu* (I swear). The meaning is: indeed the oath by the setting-places of the stars is a mighty oath, if you knew."

Then He mentioned the thing sworn to, saying: ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, meaning: Allah honoured it, made it mighty, and raised its status above all the Books. He made it noble above being sorcery, soothsaying, or lies. It was also said that it is noble because of the noble characteristics and lofty matters it contains. It was also said that it is because it honours its memorizer and magnifies its reciter.

Al-Wāḥidī related from the people of meanings (*ahl al-maʿānī*) that the description of the Qur'an as *karīm* (noble) is because it is in its nature to give abundant good through the proofs that lead to the truth in religion. Al-Azharī said: *al-karīm* is a comprehensive term for what is praiseworthy, and the Qur'an is noble, praised for the guidance, clarification, knowledge and wisdom it contains.

﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾, meaning hidden and protected. It was said: safeguarded from falsehood, and this is the *al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ* (the Preserved Tablet), as a group said. It was also said that it is a book. ʿIkrimah said: it is the Torah and the Gospel, in which the Qur'an and the one to whom it is revealed are mentioned. Al-Suddī said: it is the Psalms (*al-Zabūr*). Mujāhid and Qatādah said: it is the codex (*muṣḥaf*) that is in our hands.

﴿None touches it but the purified﴾. Al-Wāḥidī said: most exegetes hold that the pronoun refers to the Book that is well-guarded, meaning: none touches the Book that is well-guarded except the purified, and they are the angels. It was said they are the angels and the messengers from among the children of Adam. The meaning of "does not touch it" is actual touching. It was also said its meaning is: none descends with it except the purified. It was said its meaning is: none recites it. On the view that the intended Book is the Qur'an, it was said that ﴿None touches it but the purified﴾ means: purified from ritual impurities (*aḥdāth*) and filth (*anjās*). So said Qatādah and others. al-Kalbī said: "the purified" are those purified from *shirk* (polytheism). al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: those purified from sins and faults. Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl and others said: the meaning of ﴿does not touch it﴾ is: none recites it except the purified, that is, except the monotheists (*al-muwaḥḥidūn*). al-Farrāʾ said: none obtains its benefit and blessing except the purified, that is, the believers. al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl said: none knows its interpretation and explanation except one whom Allah has purified from *shirk* and hypocrisy.

The majority held that one in a state of ritual impurity (*muḥdith*) is forbidden from touching the codex (*muṣḥaf*). This was said by ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Saʿīd ibn Zayd, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Zuhrī, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥakam, Ḥammād, and a group of jurists, among them Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Shaʿbī, and a group including Abū Ḥanīfah that it is permissible for the one in a state of ritual impurity to touch it. We have clarified what is the truth in this matter in our commentary on *al-Muntaqā*, so let one refer to it.

The majority recited ﴿al-muṭahharūn﴾ with a light *ṭāʾ* and a heavy *hāʾ* with a fatḥah, as a passive participle (*ism mafʿūl*). Salmān al-Fārisī recited it with a kasrah on the *hāʾ*, as an active participle (*ism fāʿil*), meaning: those who purify themselves. Nāfiʿ, and Ibn ʿUmar in one narration from him, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, recited it with a sukūn on the *ṭāʾ* and a fatḥah on the *hāʾ*, lightly, as a passive participle from *aṭhara*. al-Ḥasan, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf recited it with a heavy *ṭāʾ* and a kasrah on the *hāʾ*, and its original form is *al-mutaṭahharūn*.

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. The majority recited it in the nominative (*rafʿ*), and it was also recited in the accusative (*naṣb*). The nominative is because it is another adjective of *qurʾān*, or the predicate of an omitted subject, while the accusative is as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*).

﴿Then is it this discourse that you are scornful of?﴾ The demonstrative refers to the Qur'an, described by the preceding attributes. The *mudhin* and *mudāhin* are the hypocrite. So said al-Zajjāj and others. ʿAṭāʾ and others said: it is the liar. Muqātil ibn Sulaymān and Qatādah said: *mudhinūn* means disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9]. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: *mudhinūn* means those who turn away. Mujāhid said: those who side with the disbelievers in disbelief. Abū Kaysān said: *al-mudhin* is one who does not recognise the right of Allah upon him and wards it off with excuses.

The first view is preferable, because the origin of *mudhin* is one whose outward appearance differs from his inward reality, as if he resembles oil (*duhn*) in its smoothness. al-Muʾarrij said: *al-mudhin* is the hypocrite who softens in order to conceal his disbelief. *Al-idhān* and *al-mudāhanah* are denial, disbelief and hypocrisy. Its origin is softness, and to conceal the opposite of what one displays. In *al-Kashshāf* it is said: *mudhinūn*, meaning: those who are lax regarding it, like one who "*yudhin*" in a matter, that is, who softens his side and does not stand firm in it out of laxity regarding it. End of quote.

al-Rāghib said: *al-idhān* originally is like *al-tadhīn* (anointing with oil), but it has become an expression for flattery (*al-mudārāh*) and softness (*al-mulāyanah*), and abandoning seriousness, just as *al-taqrīd* (removing ticks) became an expression for that. What he mentioned is supported by the saying of Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat:

"Resolve and strength are better than flattery, and the timid and the cowardly."

﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ There is an omitted genitive (*muḍāf maḥdhūf*) in the speech, as al-Wāḥidī related from the exegetes, meaning: you make the thanks for your provision that you deny the blessing of Allah, so you place denial in the place of thanks. Al-Haytham said: the Azd Shanūʾah say *mā ruziqa fulānun*, meaning: "he did not give thanks." According to this dialect, there is no omitted genitive in the verse, rather the meaning of *rizq* (provision) is thanks. The reason for expressing thanks by *rizq* is that thanks overflows with an increase of provision, so thanks becomes a provision, expressing the cause by the effect (*taʿbīr bil-sabab ʿan al-musabbab*). Among what falls under this verse is the saying of the disbelievers when Allah gives them drink and sends rain down upon them: "We were given drink by such-and-such a star, and we were given rain by such-and-such a star."

al-Azharī said: the meaning of the verse is: instead of thanking Him, you make your provision, which Allah has provided you, the denial that it is from Allah the Provider.

ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās recited *wa-tajʿalūna shukrakum* ("and you make your thanks"). The majority recited ﴿annakum tukadhdhibūn﴾ with a doubled *dhāl* from *al-takdhīb* (denial), while ʿAlī and ʿĀṣim, in one narration from him, recited it with a light *dhāl* from *al-kadhib* (lying).

﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat﴾, meaning: then why not, when the soul or the self reaches the throat at death. No reference to it has preceded, because the meaning is understood by them when they use such an expression. From this is the saying of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī:

"O Māwiyyah, wealth does not avail a man when the death-rattle takes him one day and the chest constricts upon it."

﴿And you at that moment are looking on﴾, at what he is in, that one whose soul or spirit has reached the throat.

al-Zajjāj said: "And you, O people of the dead, in that state, see the dead one as he has come to the point of his soul leaving. The meaning is that in that state they cannot repel it from him, and they cannot do anything that benefits him or lightens what he is in."

﴿And We are nearer to him than you﴾, meaning by knowledge, power and sight.
